title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra

title: Adhyātmamataparīkṣā
summary: Yaśovijaya's Prakrit-Sanskrit critique of the Adhyātma movement of Banārsīdās's followers: against its niścaya-only reading and its Digambara positions (e.g. that the kevalin does not eat).

title: Adhyātmasāra
summary: Yaśovijaya's c. 950-verse Sanskrit work in seven parts on adhyātma: its definition as pure activity centred on the self, the renunciation of hypocrisy, the nature of saṃsāra, three kinds of detachment (born of pain, of delusion, of knowledge), equanimity, right view, yoga as action and knowledge, meditation and self-experience.

title: Adhyātmopaniṣad
summary: Yaśovijaya's Sanskrit verse treatise in four sections on the yoga of scripture, of knowledge, of action and of equanimity, holding knowledge and ritual action together.

notes: The debate continued: Rāmācārya's Taraṅgiṇī (Dvaita) answered it; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā (Gauḍa-Brahmānandī) replied to the Taraṅgiṇī.
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's great dialectical defence of Advaita (four chapters) against Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta, answering it point by point in Navya-Nyāya language: the falsity (mithyātva) of the world under five definitions, the inference 'the world is false because it is seen, insentient and limited', indescribable ignorance, the partless meaning of the mahāvākya, the means and liberation.

summary: Yāmuna's defence of the Vedic authority of the Pāñcarātra. Contrasting it with the 'Māheśvara' tantras, he names four Śaiva groups - Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas - and reports the Kāpālika six insignia and yoni-meditation, the Kālāmukha skull and corpse-ash practices, the Pāśupata five categories, and the claim that initiation makes one a brahmin at once; he judges all of them outside the Veda.

alt_summary: Yāmuna's treatise establishing the validity (prāmāṇya) of the Pāñcarātra: it sets out the objections — that the Pāñcarātra is outside the Veda, that its followers (Sātvatas/Bhāgavatas) are a low temple-serving caste, that Bādarāyaṇa refuted it — and answers that it was spoken by the omniscient Lord, is Vedic in root, and that its followers are brahmins; it distinguishes it from the Śaiva schools (Kāpālika, Kālāmukha, Pāśupata, Śaiva).

title: Akulavīratantra
summary: A short tantra in two recensions praising the Akulavīra — the one reality beyond all distinctions, the same in everything, beyond mind, caste, ritual, fasting and pilgrimage. summary: The principal text of a rājayoga called 'mindlessness' (amanaska): by a gaze without object and the guru's grace the mind dissolves effortlessly, the breath stops of itself and the yogin attains liberation while living. Its second chapter dismisses laborious methods — breath-control, mudrās, mantra-repetition, meditation on objects, pilgrimage, scriptural study — as useless or harmful beside this natural state.

Several of its verses reappear in the Haṭhapradīpikā.

title: Amaraughaśāsana
summary: A prose treatise ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, printed in the Kashmir Series with a commentary. It sets out the elements, breaths, channels, ten doors and seven bonds of the body, locates the 'desire, poison and spotless' (kāma, viṣa, nirañjana) at the root of the brahma-staff, rejects rival definitions of liberation (cutting off karma, Veda-recitation, the supportless, meditation on form, bindu and nāda, Kaula union, the movement of kuṇḍalinī) and defines liberation as the mind seeing the mind in sahaja-samādhi.

canon.group_scheme: editorial grouping of the 108 used by the Adyar Library series and most modern catalogues; the Muktikā itself lists the 108 by Veda only

attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Mind is the cause of bondage and liberation — attached to objects it binds, free of them it frees; restrain it in the heart till it dissolves; the one self appears many like the moon in water and is limited like space in a pot; beyond śabda-brahman lies the supreme; closes 'I am Vāsudeva'.

title: Amṛtānubhava (Anubhavāmṛta)
summary: Jñāneśvar's independent work on non-dual experience: after saluting Śiva and Śakti as one and praising his guru Nivṛtti, it argues that the words sat, cit and ānanda, the word itself, ignorance and even knowledge fail before the self-luminous reality, which sports as the world; it ends in a devotion in which God, devotee and worship are one.

attribution.tradition: Written at Nivṛttināth's bidding as an independent work (svatantra grantha) after the commentary.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted as Jñāneśvar's.

tradition.text: shortly after the Jñāneśvarī

structure.description: 10 chapters (prakaraṇas), about 800 ovīs

title: Amṛtarasāvalī

attribution.tradition: anonymous or not recalled
attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text on the nectar of rasa and the stages of the sahaja path (attributed in some accounts to Mukunda's circle; low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Amṛtaratnāvalī

attribution.tradition: attributed to mukunda dasa sahajiya
attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A principal Sahajiyā manual attributed to Mukunda Dāsa: the sahaja mānuṣa within, the distinction of rūpa and svarūpa, the practice of āropa, the stages of the path and the ideal of parakīyā love (in coded language).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Amṛtasiddhi

attribution.tradition: ascribed in its colophon/Tibetan transmission to Virūpākṣa (identified with the Buddhist mahāsiddha Virūpa)
attribution.scholarly: anonymous Buddhist tantric (Vajrayāna) milieu with Śaiva elements; authorship uncertain

scholarly.text: c. 11th c. CE; a manuscript dated 1160 CE gives a terminus ante quem

structure.description: 36 short chapters (viveka) — c. 300 verses (as recalled; check the Mallinson–Szántó edition)

summary: The earliest known text to teach the methods later called haṭha: bindu, identified with the moon in the head, is the essence of life and is consumed by the sun (fire) in the belly; by mahāmudrā, mahābandha and mahāvedha the breath is forced into the central channel, bindu is made steady and the yogin attains the 'nectar of immortality'. It also first teaches the four stages (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti). Its setting is Buddhist tantric, with Śaiva elements.

editions.name: J. Mallinson & P.-D. Szántó, The Amṛtasiddhi and Amṛtasiddhimūla: the earliest texts of the haṭhayoga tradition (Pondicherry: IFP/EFEO 2021)

notes: Chapter count and attribution recalled, not checked: low confidence on details. U49 documents the Buddhist→haṭha borrowing.

title: Amṛtasiddhimūla
alt_titles: bdud rtsi grub pa'i rtsa ba (Tibetan, Tōh 2285)

attribution.tradition: The Derge colophon (145a.1) reads 'the Amṛtasiddhi composed by the great master Virūpa is complete' and says it was translated by an Indian master, a yogin who had attained siddhi (name read uncertainly)
attribution.scholarly: a short text closely related to the Amṛtasiddhi, edited with it by Mallinson & Szántó (2021)

summary: In the Derge Tengyur (Tōh 2285, among the siddhas' works of vol. zhi) the text opens with homage to Śrī Heruka and to a three-eyed, head-severed, red deity who dispels the fear of death, then announces the 'great seals' (phyag rgya chen po) and teaches the seated seal with the heel at the perineum — the mahāmudrā of the early haṭha texts — in a Buddhist tantric frame.

alt_summary: A brief companion ('root') text of the Amṛtasiddhi on the same bindu-centred yoga; contents not recalled in detail.
alt_notes: Existence recalled from the title of the 2021 edition; contents to be supplied in Phase C/D.

title: Aṃśumadāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Ambu (Kiraṇa: Aṃśu), then Agra (Kiraṇa: Ugra), then Ravi (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Śivabheda no. 9 in the Kāmika's order; 12 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: Aṃśumatkāśyapāgama, IFP transcript (Muktabodha M00198)

notes: Kiraṇa 10.6/10.11: Aṃśu → Ugra → Ravi. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Aṃśumat'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the back (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 9 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Śivabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Ambu (Kiraṇa: Aṃśu), then Agra (Kiraṇa: Ugra), then Ravi. The Kāmika assigns it 12 upabheda(s): Vidyāpurāṇatantra, Vāsava, Nīlalohita, Prakāraṇa, Bhūtatantra, Ātmālaṅkāra, Kāśyapa, Gautama, Aindra, Brāhma, Vāsiṣṭha, Aiśāna. Known especially for chapters on temple architecture and iconography.

title: The Mahāmudrā of the Amulet Box
summary: Niguma's Mahāmudrā instruction: the ground, path and fruit 'enclosed together like the two halves of an amulet box'; the three self-liberations, the four faults self-liberated, and the four kāyas as fruition.

title: Anādi-pātana
summary: Assamese account of creation and the cosmic cycle, drawn from the Bhāgavata and Vāmana Purāṇa.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

summary: A Sanskrit compendium of the 'beginningless' Vīraśaiva dharma that opens with homage to Guru Basava-liṅga and to Prabhu (Allama).

summary: On the unimaginable beginning of saṃsāra: more tears shed than the water of the four oceans (15.3), mothers beyond counting (15.1).

title: Ānandabhairava

attribution.tradition: anonymous or not recalled
attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text, perhaps framed as a dialogue of deities, on rasa and the sahaja path (low confidence on content).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Ānandabhāṣya
summary: A commentary on the Brahma Sūtras (with related commentaries on the Gītā and Upaniṣads) attributed to Rāmānanda by the Rāmānandīs who assert the sect's independence from the Śrīvaiṣṇavas; it reads the Sūtras as teaching a qualified non-dualism centred on Rāma.

attribution.tradition: Rāmānanda's own commentary, recovered and published in the 20th century.
attribution.scholarly: Widely regarded as a 20th-century composition connected with the Rāmānandī independence movement; not attested earlier.

title: Ānandaghana-aṣṭapadī
summary: Yaśovijaya's eight Gujarati/Hindi verses in praise of Ānandaghana, which the tradition takes as a record of their meeting.

title: Ānandaghana Bahottarī
summary: Seventy-two (more in some collections) devotional-mystical padas in old Hindi attributed to Ānandaghana: the avadhūta who knows the self beyond sects and names, the soul-bride awaiting her lord, and inner experience (anubhava).
notes: Attribution of individual padas varies between collections (low confidence on any given pada).

title: Ānandaghana Covīsī
summary: Ānandaghana's hymns (stavana) to the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in old Gujarati-Rajasthani (he completed twenty-two; later poets supplied the last two): the soul's love-longing for the Jina as its only beloved, the difficulty of the true path, and the six darśanas as the limbs of the Jina.
notes: Language given as old Gujarati-Rajasthani (Marugurjara). Commented by Jñānavimala and by Śrīmad Rājacandra's circle (recalled).

title: Ānandagiri's gloss on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya
summary: Ānandagiri's sub-commentary explaining Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya; it frames the first and middle hexads as teaching the meanings of 'thou' and 'that' and the last hexad as teaching the meaning of the sentence (their identity).

title: Ātmakhyāti
summary: Amṛtacandra's Sanskrit commentary on Kundakunda's Samayasāra, which reads the text through the pure standpoint and embeds some 278 verses (the kalaśas).
alt_summary: Amṛtacandra's Sanskrit commentary on the Samayasāra, interspersed with the verses (kalaśa) later collected as the Samayasāra-kalaśa; the classic reading of Kundakunda's standpoint of ultimate reality.

title: Ātmānātmaviveka

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkara
attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A catechetical prose treatise discriminating the self from the not-self (body, senses, sheaths).

title: Ātmānuśāsana
summary: Guṇabhadra's c. 270 verses of self-admonition urging detachment and austerity.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:आत्मानुशासन--आ-गुणभद्र); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Ātmaprakāśa

attribution.tradition: Śrīdhara's commentary on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
attribution.scholarly: Printed with the Viṣṇucittīya.

notes: Named in the heading of the local e-text ('viṣṇucittyātmaprakāśākhyaśrīdharīya vyākhyādvayopetam').
summary: Śrīdhara's gloss on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

checks.note: Named in the heading of the local VP e-text ('viṣṇucittyātmaprakāśākhyaśrīdharīya vyākhyādvayopetam'); web confirms Śrīdhara's commentary on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

title: Ātmapurāṇa
summary: Śaṅkarānanda's long verse retelling of the teaching of the Upaniṣads in narrative form.

title: Ātmasiddhi Śāstra

structure.description: 142 dohās

summary: Śrīmad Rājacandra's 142 Gujarati dohās (1896) establishing the six fundamentals — the soul exists, is eternal, is the doer and the enjoyer of its karma, liberation exists and there is a means to it — with the marks of the true teacher (sadguru) and of the sectarian (matārthī) and the self-seeker (ātmārthī).
notes: Registry id. Tradition: written in one sitting for Saubhāgbhāī and a few close disciples.

title: Ātmatattvaviveka
summary: Udayana's defence of an enduring self against Buddhist positions, organized as refutations of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), of the denial of external objects (bāhyārthabhaṅga), of the denial of the difference between quality and qualified (guṇaguṇibhedabhaṅga), and of the argument from the non-apprehension of a self (anupalambha); it closes with the knowledge of the self and liberation.
notes: Commented on by Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (Dīdhiti) and Mathurānātha. The alternative title is recalled, not checked.

title: Ātmatattvavivekadīdhiti
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's commentary on Udayana's Ātmatattvaviveka.

title: Ātmavidyāvilāsa
summary: Sadāśiva Brahmendra's verses on the conduct and inner state of the avadhūta knower of the self.

title: Atrismṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Atri, one of the twenty lawgivers named by Yājñavalkya (1.4–5).
notes: Contents not summarized here — gap.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as extant. Atri is one of the twenty lawgivers of YājñS 1.4–5 (text-located).

title: Attakārī Sutta
summary: To a brahmin who holds that one does not act by one's own or another's doing, the Buddha points to the elements of initiative, persistence and exertion.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Aṭṭhakavagga
summary: The fourth vagga of the Sutta Nipāta (16 poems): the sage (muni) who clings to no view, does not dispute, is free of sensual desire and of 'mine', and does not take a stand on purity by views, rules or vows.

scholarly.text: among the oldest Buddhist texts; a Chinese parallel (Arthapada, T 198) exists

title: Atthasālinī

attribution.tradition: rendered into Pali from the Sinhala commentaries (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, Mahāpaccarī, Kurundī and others) of the Mahāvihāra
attribution.scholarly: the extant Pali commentaries date from the 5th–6th c. and preserve older Sinhala material

summary: Buddhaghosa's commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī; its introduction (Nidānakathā) defends the Abhidhamma as the Buddha's word and tells how it was taught in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; the body explains consciousness, the mental factors, matter and the five niyāmas.
notes: Cūḷavaṃsa reports that Buddhaghosa wrote an 'Atthasālinī' in India before coming to Lanka; the extant text cites the Visuddhimagga (tradition's account vs. text's evidence noted).

title: Āturapratyākhyāna
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the renunciation made by the sick or dying (ātura): the kinds of death (of the ignorant, of the partly wise, of the wise) and the preparation of mind for a peaceful death (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Aucityavicāracarcā of Kṣemendra
summary: Kṣemendra's essay making propriety (aucitya) the life of rasa-filled poetry, illustrated with good and bad examples.

title: Aupapātika Sūtra
summary: The first Upāṅga (paired with the Ācārāṅga): a model description of the city of Campā, of Mahāvīra's arrival, his assembly and King Kūṇika's visit, his sermon, the kinds of ascetics and the heavens they are reborn in (upapāta), the wanderer Ambaḍa and his disciples, and the state of the liberated (siddha).

attribution.tradition: An aṅgabāhya text composed by the elders (sthavira)

title: Avadhūta Gītā

attribution.tradition: sung by Dattātreya, the avadhūta; the closing verse (8.28) names 'Dattātreya the Avadhūta' as its maker; one colophon speaks of a dialogue of Svāmī and Kārttika, remembered as disciples who recorded it
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; date and provenance uncertain

tradition.text: sung by the avatāra Dattātreya (mythic time)

scholarly.text: uncertain; generally placed in the late first or early second millennium CE

structure.description: 8 chapters, c. 289 verses (1: 76, 2: 40, 3: 46, 4: 25, 5: 32, 6: 27, 7: 15, 8: 28 in the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha edition)

summary: An ecstatic statement of non-duality from the standpoint of the realized: only by the Lord's grace does the inclination to non-duality arise; the self alone is, formless and all-pervading; there is no one to bow to, no bondage or liberation, no meditator and meditated. Chapter 8 defines the avadhūta syllable by syllable, repeats the Bhāgavata's list of the sage's virtues and warns the renunciant against sexual association and drink.

editions.name: Gītāsaṅgraha (Poona 1915), eBhāratī Sampat Ebharati-6673
Avadhūtagītā with commentary, eBhāratī Sampat (gItAH/anyagItA/dattAtreyaH)

notes: Avadhūta Gītā 8.2-4 reproduce Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.29-31 (the qualities of the sage) almost verbatim. Chapter 8 differs in tone from 1-7; whether it is a later addition is not settled here (see REPORT).

checks.note: 8 chapters of 76,40,46,25,32,27,15,28 = 289 verses, verified exactly in the 1915 Gītāsaṅgraha. 8.28 names 'dattātreyāvadhūta' as maker, and the 8th-chapter colophon names the Svāmī-Kārttika dialogue. Wikipedia (after Abhayananda) puts it in the 9th-10th c., which fits the entry's 'late first or early second millennium'.

title: Āvaśyaka Niryukti
summary: The Prakrit verse commentary (niryukti) on the Āvaśyaka, the most important of the ten niryuktis ascribed to Bhadrabāhu: besides explaining terms by the method of nikṣepa it narrates the lives of Ṛṣabha and Mahāvīra, the gaṇadharas' doubts and the schisms (nihnava), and states that the Arhat speaks the meaning and the gaṇadharas compose the sūtras.

attribution.tradition: Bhadrabāhu, the śrutakevalin
attribution.scholarly: a later Bhadrabāhu or anonymous authors, c. 1st–6th c. CE

title: Āvaśyaka Sūtra
summary: The Mūlasūtra of the six obligatory daily duties (āvaśyaka): equanimity (sāmāyika), praise of the twenty-four Jinas (caturviṃśatistava, the 'Logassa'), veneration of the teacher (vandana), confession and repentance (pratikramaṇa), abandoning the body in standing meditation (kāyotsarga), and renunciation of specified things for a set time (pratyākhyāna). Its formulas, beginning with the Namaskāra, are the core of Jain liturgy; its niryukti and commentaries carry much narrative.

structure.description: 6 chapters (the six āvaśyakas)

title: Āvaśyaka-vṛtti of Haribhadra
summary: Haribhadra's commentary (Śiṣyahitā) on the Āvaśyaka and its niryukti, among the earliest Sanskrit commentaries on the canon; Haribhadra also commented on the Daśavaikālika, Nandī and Anuyogadvāra.

title: Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra
summary: The 'Flower Ornament' sūtra: a vast compilation in which the Buddha, just awakened, is revealed as Vairocana filling the dharmadhātu; bodhisattvas describe the interpenetration of all worlds in each atom, the stages of the bodhisattva path (ten abodes, practices, dedications, grounds), the 'arising of the Tathāgata' present in all beings, Samantabhadra's practices, and, in its final part (the Gaṇḍavyūha), Sudhana's pilgrimage.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni (tradition's account: buddhavacana) in the weeks after his awakening, in seven places and eight (60-fasc.) or nine (80-fasc.) assemblies; Huayan: the first teaching, spoken as by the sun to the high mountains; legend: kept by the nāgas and brought by Nāgārjuna
attribution.scholarly: A compilation of originally independent sūtras (Daśabhūmika, Gaṇḍavyūha and others), assembled perhaps in Central Asia (Khotan), c. 3rd-4th c.

tradition.text: the second and third weeks after the awakening (Huayan)

scholarly.text: components 1st-3rd c.; compilation c. 4th c.; Chinese 418-421 and 695-699

structure.description: 60-fascicle: 34 chapters in 8 assemblies; 80-fascicle: 39 chapters in 9 assemblies; Tibetan: 45 chapters

attribution.scholarly: Usually dated c. 9th-10th c. CE and located in the Tamil south, in the milieu of the Āḻvārs; its style is deliberately archaic. Opponents of the text once alleged authorship by the 13th-c. grammarian Vopadeva (see dsp:which-bhagavata-is-the-mahapurana).

scholarly.text: layers from the mid 1st millennium CE to the 19th c. CE

summary: The Bījak ('treasure-map, inventory') is the scripture of the Kabīr Chaurā line: ramainīs on creation, māyā and delusion; śabdas that satirize paṇḍit and mullā, yogī and ascetic, and call the sants to see; sākhī couplets on the Word, the guru, death and discernment (pārakh). Its tone is sharply critical and apophatic, stressing testing and discernment over devotional sweetness.

title: Brahma Sūtra

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas × 4 pādas. Śaṅkara's recension: 555 sūtras (pāda counts 31, 32, 43, 28 | 37, 45, 53, 22 | 27, 41, 66, 52 | 19, 21, 16, 22). Other schools divide and number differently: Rāmānuja 545 sūtras, Madhva 564; Nimbārka 549 and Vallabha 554 (these two counts low confidence). Adhikaraṇa counts also differ (Śaṅkara c. 191–192; Rāmānuja c. 156; Madhva c. 223 — low confidence).

editions.name: numerous Devanāgarī editions with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya (e.g. Nirṇaya Sāgara)

notes: Pāda themes (per Śaṅkara): 1.1 texts with clear marks of Brahman; 1.2 unclear marks, Brahman as object of meditation; 1.3 unclear marks, Brahman as object of knowledge; 1.4 doubtful words (avyakta, ajā) claimed by Sāṃkhya; 2.1 objections from smṛti (Sāṃkhya, Yoga) and reason answered; 2.2 critique of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhists, Jains, Pāśupatas and (per Śaṅkara) Pāñcarātra; 2.3 creation of the elements and nature of the jīva; 2.4 the prāṇas; 3.1 transmigration (for dispassion); 3.2 the states of the self and the nature of Brahman; 3.3 combination of meditations; 3.4 auxiliaries of knowledge and the āśramas; 4.1 repetition and the effects of knowledge; 4.2 departure at death; 4.3 the path of the gods; 4.4 the liberated state. All sūtra numbers in this shard follow Śaṅkara's numbering.
summary: Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms systematizing the Upaniṣads in four adhyāyas — samanvaya (all Upaniṣadic texts converge on Brahman), avirodha (no conflict with smṛti, reason or rival systems, which are critiqued in 2.2), sādhana (transmigration, the states of the self, the meditations, the auxiliaries of knowledge) and phala (repetition of meditation, the knower's freedom from karma, departure, the path of the gods, the liberated state). Every Vedānta school is founded on a commentary on it.

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Bhāskara (Bhāskarabhāṣya)

summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, opening with the 'adhyāsa-bhāṣya' on superimposition as the root of all empirical dealings; it reads the sūtras as teaching the non-dual Brahman, the unreality of the world apart from Brahman, knowledge alone as the means to liberation, and liberation while living, and it critiques Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, the Buddhist schools, the Jains, the Pāśupatas and the Pāñcarātra.

title: Bṛhajjātaka
summary: Varāhamihira's classic of horoscopy: definitions of signs, planets and houses (with Greek-derived terms), conception and birth, infant mortality, longevity (with rival teachers' methods), planetary periods, aṣṭakavarga, livelihood, royal and nābhasa yogas, lunar and two-planet yogas, the yogas for renunciation (pravrajyā), character by signs and asterisms, aspects, houses, female nativities, the manner of death and the world one goes to next, lost horoscopes and the decans. It opens by saying the horā reveals the ripening of karma earned in a former birth.

attribution.tradition: composed by Varāhamihira of Avanti, son and pupil of Ādityadāsa, who received a boon from the Sun at Kāpitthaka, after studying the views of the seers (28.9)

title: Candrajñānāgama (Vīraśaiva recension)

title: Candrāvalokana

title: Candravedhyaka
summary: A Prakīrṇaka counted in some lists: on the qualities of teacher and pupil, discipline and concentration at death, with the image of the archer who must pierce the eye of a revolving doll (candravedhya) as a figure for unwavering attention.

title: Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī

title: Caraka Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: The teaching of Punarvasu Ātreya set down by his disciple Agniveśa, redacted (pratisaṃskṛta) by Caraka and completed by Dṛḍhabala of Pañcanada, who supplied seventeen chapters of the Cikitsā and the Kalpa and Siddhi sections (Ca Si 12.36-40); Caraka is a partial incarnation of Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa).
attribution.scholarly: A layered text: an older Agniveśa core, Caraka's redaction and Dṛḍhabala's supplement (c. 4th–5th c. CE).

tradition.text: Ātreya's teaching at the assembly of sages in the Himalaya, in a former age

scholarly.text: Caraka's redaction c. 1st c. BCE – 2nd c. CE; Dṛḍhabala c. 4th–5th c. CE

structure.description: Eight sthānas, 120 chapters (Ca Sū 30.33): Sūtra/Śloka 30, Nidāna 8, Vimāna 8, Śārīra 8, Indriya 12, Cikitsā 30, Kalpa 12, Siddhi 12

summary: The foundational compendium of internal medicine: Ātreya's teaching to Agniveśa in dialogues and assemblies of sages. It sets out the aim and definition of Āyurveda, the doṣas, dhātus and malas, diet, daily and seasonal routine and good conduct, the causes and diagnosis of disease, the examination of patient and physician, debate, the person and its constituents, embryology, the signs of death, therapeutics including rejuvenation and virility, and purificatory therapies; and it teaches a doctrine of the self, rebirth, yoga and liberation (Sū 11; Śā 1, 5).

editions.name: ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya with Cakrapāṇi's Āyurvedadīpikā (Bombay, Nirnaya Sagar 1941 and reprints)

title: Caraṇavyūha
summary: A short treatise listing the branches (śākhās, caraṇas) of the four Vedas and their extent — e.g. the five Ṛgveda śākhās (Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana) — ascribed to Śaunaka or Kātyāyana; the Atharvaveda has its own Caraṇavyūha among its Pariśiṣṭas.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka (or Kātyāyana)
attribution.scholarly: late compilation; its counts of śākhās are traditional

notes: Ascription and exact lists recalled from memory; to be checked.

checks.note: Confirmed: 'Śaunaka's Caraṇavyūha' names five Ṛgveda śākhās — Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana (edition with Mahidāsa's commentary). The alternative ascription to Kātyāyana was not confirmed. The Atharvaveda's own Caraṇavyūha (AVPariś 49) is located locally; note that it lists SEVEN Ṛgveda śākhās (āśvalāyana, śāṅkhāyana, sādhyāyana, śākala, bāṣkala, audumbara, māṇḍūka), so 'five' applies only to Śaunaka's text.

Confirmed: the Caraṇavyūha lists the śākhās and the four upavedas. The fourth is Sthāpatya/Śilpaveda in the Caraṇavyūha, Arthaśāstra in other lists (Dharmawiki; Hindupedia), which fits the entry's 'statecraft/architecture' hedge. Wikipedia ascribes it to Śaunaka; the entry leaves this unasserted. U01 found AV Pariśiṣṭa 49 to be a Caraṇavyūha.

alt_summary: A short supplement (pariśiṣṭa) listing the branches (śākhā) of the four Vedas and the auxiliary sciences, including the four Upavedas — medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft/architecture — attached to the four Vedas.
alt_notes: The assignment of the fourth Upaveda (arthaśāstra or sthāpatyaveda) varies between sources; attribution (Śaunaka?) not asserted.

title: Darśanasāra of Devasena
summary: Devasena's short Prakrit account (Vikrama 990 = 933 CE, at Dhārā) of the origin of 'false doctrines' (darśana) — Buddhism, Śvetāmbaras, Yāpanīyas, the Drāviḍa, Kāṣṭhā and Māthura saṅghas and others — each with a founder and a date; it also mentions Padmanandin (Kundakunda) receiving knowledge from Sīmandhara.

title: Daśabhakti
summary: Ten devotional hymns (to the Siddhas, scripture, conduct, the yogins, the ācāryas, nirvāṇa and others) used in Digambara liturgy; the Sanskrit set is ascribed to Pūjyapāda.

title: Daśabhūmika-sūtra
summary: The Sūtra of the Ten Grounds, spoken by the bodhisattva Vajragarbha: the ten stages (bhūmi) of the bodhisattva from Joyful (pramuditā) to Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), each with its perfection, purifications and attainments; in the sixth ground the three realms are 'mind only' and the twelve links depend on mind; at the eighth, Immovable, the bodhisattva attains the acceptance of non-arising and is roused by the buddhas not to enter peace.
alt_titles: Shidi jing 十地經 / Shidi pin (Avataṃsaka ch. 22 (60) / 26 (80))

title: Daśabhūmikavyākhyāna

title: Daśarūpaka of Dhanañjaya

summary: Nimbārka's ten verses summarising the school: the soul, bondage and release, the three kinds of non-conscious reality, Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā, worship, the reality of all as Brahman's nature, refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, grace and devotion, and the five things to be known.

title: Daśāśrutaskandha
summary: A Chedasūtra in ten chapters: the twenty faults disturbing concentration (asamādhi-sthāna), the twenty-one grave faults (śabala), the thirty-three disrespects to the teacher (āśātanā), the eight accomplishments of a gaṇin, the ten states of mental concentration, the eleven stages of the layman (upāsaka-pratimā), the twelve special vows of the monk (bhikṣu-pratimā), the Paryuṣaṇākalpa (the Kalpa Sūtra), the thirty sources of deluding karma, and the nine kinds of 'wishing for a reward' (nidāna).

title: Daśavaikālika Sūtra
summary: The second Mūlasūtra, the first text learned by a new Śvetāmbara monk: dharma as non-harm, restraint and austerity; the bee that takes nectar without hurting the flower; the six classes of living beings and the vows; the rules of alms-seeking and speech; conquering the four passions; and the marks of the true monk.

summary: The first text to teach a system it calls haṭhayoga. Dattātreya names four yogas — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja (the best) — and four stages; he teaches the eight-limbed yoga 'known to Yājñavalkya and others' and the haṭha of 'Kapila and the others' (mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, the three bandhas, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī with amarolī and sahajolī). Success comes from practice to anyone — brāhmaṇa, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist.

title: Devī Māhātmya

structure.description: 13 chapters in three caritas (ch. 1; chs. 2-4; chs. 5-13). The tradition counts 700 mantras (hence 'Saptaśatī') by counting half-verses, speaker-lines and refrains; the metrical verses number c. 580-590 (588 numbered verses in the Sansknet e-text)

notes: Recited with ancillary texts (aṅgas): Kavaca, Argalā, Kīlaka before, and the three Rahasyas (Prādhānika, Vaikṛtika, Mūrti) after; the naming of the three caritas' deities as Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī comes from the dhyāna verses and the Rahasyas, not from the 13 chapters themselves. Commentaries include Bhāskararāya's Guptavatī (src:guptavati) and the Śāntanavī. Śākta theology shared with U23. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the MkP (chs. 1-93; Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81-93 in this numbering)
summary: The Goddess, Mahāmāyā, is the eternal source and power of the world who deludes even the wise and grants liberation; she wakes Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arises from the gods' combined radiance to slay Mahiṣa, and as Ambikā with Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Śumbha, Niśumbha and their generals; hymned as present in all beings ('yā devī sarvabhūteṣu'), she promises to return whenever demons oppress the world.

checks.note: Extant and digitized (MkP 81-93 in GRETIL/Sansknet; Gita Press Durgā Saptaśatī local; DCS). The 13 chapters contain exactly 588 numbered verses in the Sansknet text, as the entry says; Medhas named at 81.9. Web: DM in MkP chs. 81-93, c. 550 CE (entry 5th-6th c.).

Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. title: Dṛṣṭivāda
summary: The twelfth Aṅga, lost according to both traditions. As described in the Nandī and Samavāyāṅga it had five parts — parikarma, sūtra, pūrvagata (the fourteen Pūrvas), anuyoga (including the first narrative anuyoga) and cūlikā — and contained all doctrine. The Digambaras hold that portions of two Pūrvas survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

attribution.tradition: Composed by the gaṇadharas; the fourteen Pūrvas were known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu; Sthūlabhadra learned the last four as text only; knowledge of the Pūrvas died out gradually (Śvetāmbara: with Devarddhigaṇi's time; Digambara: within 683 years of the nirvāṇa).

attribution.tradition: Eknāth's.

title: Eknāthī Bhāgavat
summary: Eknāth's great Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Uddhava and the nine sages' teaching to Nimi): devotion to the name, the guru and the saints, the avadhūta's twenty-four teachers, and non-dual knowledge, with a defence of teaching in Marathi. attribution.tradition: Begun at Paiṭhaṇ and completed at Vārāṇasī (Maṇikarṇikā), where it was honoured by the paṇḍits.

alt_summary: A vast Marathi verse commentary on Bhāgavata Book 11 (the Uddhava Gītā), expounding devotion, the avadhūta's teachers and non-dual knowledge for the Vārkarī tradition.

title: Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra
summary: The final part of the Avataṃsaka, also an independent sūtra: sent by Mañjuśrī, the youth Sudhana visits fifty-odd spiritual friends — monks, laymen and laywomen, a courtesan, kings, goddesses of the night, a boy teacher, the Buddha's mother Māyā and wife Gopā — each teaching one liberation; Maitreya shows him the tower of Vairocana in which all worlds are reflected; he returns to Mañjuśrī and finally merges with Samantabhadra, whose vows (the Bhadracarī) conclude the text.

notes: Ācārakāṇḍa 1.142: the ten avatāras; 1.235-239 (approx.): brahma-jñāna, ātma-jñāna, Gītāsāra, Brahmagītāsāra; Pretakalpa 2.38.5: the seven liberating cities; Brahmakāṇḍa 3.1: its own sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa grading of the Purāṇas. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Garuḍa Purāṇa (Venkateshwara ed.; Pretakalpa cited as 2.chapter.verse)
summary: A Vaiṣṇava encyclopedia best known for its Pretakalpa: the process of dying, Yama's messengers, the thumb-sized person, the year-long road to Yama's city past sixteen towns and the Vaitaraṇī river, judgment, the preta state and its signs, and the rites that give the dead a body and join them to the ancestors.

summary: The classical Purāṇic manual of dying and the afterlife: the signs and pains of death, the thumb-sized person led off by Yama's messengers, the airy conveyance-body and the body built by the ten days' piṇḍas, the year-long road, the Vaitaraṇī, judgment, the preta state and its release through the sons' rites, gifts to the dying, and the means of liberation.

correction_log.reason: Located in the local 120-Upaniṣad e-text (heading at line 26171 (collection no. 106)). Its place in the Muktikā canon is confirmed from the Muktikā in the same e-text: no. 102 in 1.30-39, listed under the Atharvaveda in the prose Veda lists, with that Veda's peace-chant. Group 'Vaiṣṇava' matches the Wikipedia group list. CORRECTION to editions: the skeleton gave every text the same generator default, 'Adyar Library Upaniṣad series (Schrader … 1912; … with Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's commentary)'. Schrader's 1912 volume is a critical edition of twenty Saṃnyāsa texts with his own ṭippaṇī, not Brahmayogin's commentary. Brahmayogin's commentary on the Saṃnyāsa group appeared separately in 1929 (ed. T. R. Chintamani Dikshit; Muktabodha M00334 metadata; archive.org). The Adyar volume is therefore replaced with the one volume that holds this text (Vaiṣṇava). The years 1920, 1921, 1923 and 1925, and the editor A. Mahadeva Sastri, are confirmed on the web. The group-level scholarly dating statement is generic and was not checked text by text. The tradition account (śruti, authorless) is left as it is.

title: Gīta Govinda
summary: Jayadeva's Sanskrit song-poem in twelve cantos and twenty-four songs (aṣṭapadīs, each set to a named rāga and tāla) with linking verses: Kṛṣṇa's spring dance with the cowherd women, Rādhā's jealousy and withdrawal, the longing of both in separation carried by Rādhā's friend, Kṛṣṇa's plea for forgiveness, and their union. It opens with a hymn to the ten avatāras borne by Kṛṣṇa and offers itself to those whose minds delight in remembering Hari and in the arts of love.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (as the closing verse says), in the service of Jagannātha at Purī (Odisha account) or at the Bengal court of Lakṣmaṇasena (Bengal account); by tradition Kṛṣṇa himself wrote one line (10th canto).
attribution.scholarly: Jayadeva, 12th c. CE; the opening names poets of Lakṣmaṇasena's court (Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana, Dhoyī); his birthplace (Kenduli in Bengal or Kenduli Sasan in Odisha, or Mithilā) is disputed.

structure.description: 12 sargas (cantos) with 24 aṣṭapadī songs and interspersed ślokas; canto titles as commonly printed: Sāmoda-dāmodara, Akleśa-keśava, Mugdha-madhusūdana, Snigdha-madhusūdana, Sākāṅkṣa-puṇḍarīkākṣa, Dhṛṣṭa-vaikuṇṭha, Nāgara-nārāyaṇa, Vilakṣa-lakṣmīpati, Mugdha-mukunda, Catura-caturbhuja, Sānanda-dāmodara, Suprīta-pītāmbara (variants exist)

notes: Liturgical use: sung daily before Jagannātha at Purī (by tradition confirmed by an order of Gajapati Pratāparudra, c. 1499, that the temple singers sing only the Gīta Govinda — recalled with moderate confidence); sung in Kerala temples as aṣṭapadī (sopāna saṅgītam) and in South Indian bhajana; relished by Caitanya (Caitanya Caritāmṛta); two of Jayadeva's hymns (not from the Gīta Govinda) are in the Sikh Ādi Granth (context only). Canto-title list: moderate/low confidence. Not to be confused with the later Jayadeva (Pīyūṣavarṣa) of the Candrāloka and Prasannarāghava.

title: Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra (Guanjing shu)
alt_titles: Guanjing sitiemshu 觀經四帖疏 / Kangyō shijōsho

structure.description: 4 fascicles: the essential meaning; the introduction; the meditative good (contemplations 1–13); the non-meditative good (14–16)

summary: Shandao's commentary, written to 'settle the old and the new' interpretations: the Contemplation Sūtra was taught for ordinary beings, all nine grades are ordinary people; Sukhāvatī is a reward land into which ordinary beings are born by the Buddha's vow; the first thirteen contemplations are meditative good, the last three non-meditative good; the three minds (sincere, deep, transferring) with the two kinds of deep entrusting; the five right practices, of which the calling of the name is the rightly determined act 'because it accords with the Buddha's vow'; the parable of the two rivers and the white path; the sūtra's final entrustment of the name shows that the Buddha's intent is exclusive calling of Amitābha's name. Hōnen converted on reading it (1175).

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

title: Haṃsadūta
summary: Rūpa's messenger poem: Lalitā sends a swan to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā with Rādhā's message of separation.

title: Haṃsasandeśa
summary: Deśika's messenger poem in which Rāma sends a swan to Sītā in Laṅkā.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Handbook for Mankind (Khu Mue Manut)
summary: Buddhadāsa's lectures on the essentials: suffering, the three characteristics, 'I' and 'mine', the three trainings and nibbāna here and now.

title: Hanumān Bāhuk
summary: Forty-odd verses addressed to Hanumān, praying for relief from a painful affliction of the arm.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Tulsī in old age when his arm was afflicted; recited against pain.
attribution.scholarly: Generally accepted; sometimes treated as an appendix to the Kavitāvalī.

tradition.text: Tulsīdās's lifetime (tradition: born Saṃvat 1554 / 1497 CE, died Saṃvat 1680 / 1623 CE)

title: Hanumān Cālīsā
summary: Forty caupāīs framed by dohās praising Hanumān as Rāma's servant, messenger and remover of obstacles; opens by cleansing the mirror of the mind with the dust of the guru's feet. The most widely recited Hindi devotional text.

attribution.tradition: Tulsīdās's.
attribution.scholarly: Not among the twelve works accepted in early lists; the attribution is uncertain.

structure.description: 2 opening dohās, 40 caupāīs, 1 closing dohā

title: Hārāmaṇi
genre: collection of folk and Bāul songs

attribution.tradition: the 'lost jewels' of Bengali folk song collected by Muhammad Mansuruddin
attribution.scholarly: 13 volumes from 1931

summary: Muhammad Mansuruddin's great collection of Bengali folk songs including many Bāul and Lalon songs, a principal printed witness for the oral corpus.

title: Haribhaktivilāsa
summary: The Gauḍīya code of Vaiṣṇava ritual and conduct in twenty 'vilāsas': the guru and disciple and their testing, initiation, daily purity and worship, deity worship with nyāsa and bhūta-śuddhi, the name and offences, the Ekādaśī fast and festivals, temple construction and consecration.

attribution.tradition: compiled by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa (named in the text) with Sanātana's commentary Digdarśinī; some accounts credit Sanātana with the compilation itself
attribution.scholarly: authorship division disputed

structure.description: 20 vilāsas

title: Vāṇī of Haridās Nirañjanī

attribution.tradition: the verses of Haridās Nirañjanī

summary: Verses of the founder of the Nirañjanī sampradāya on Nirañjan, yoga and devotion.

title: Harikathāmṛtasāra
summary: Jagannātha Dāsa's Kannada poem setting out Dvaita theology — Hari's supremacy, the gradation of souls and deities, the Lord's presence in all things and the means of liberation — in the Haridāsa tradition.
notes: Owned in substance by U56 (Karnataka Haridāsas); listed here for its Dvaita doctrine.

title: Harināmāmṛtavyākaraṇa
summary: Jīva's Sanskrit grammar in which every technical term is replaced by names of Kṛṣṇa, so that learning grammar is remembering the Lord.

title: Haripāṭh (of Jñāneśvar)
summary: Twenty-seven (in some editions twenty-eight) abhaṅgas on reciting the name of Hari, recited daily by Vārkarīs: the name needs no rule of time, place or caste; standing a moment at God's door wins the four liberations.

attribution.tradition: Jñāneśvar's.
attribution.scholarly: Traditional attribution; not seriously contested but linked to the abhaṅga-authorship question.

structure.description: 27 or 28 abhaṅgas

notes: Nāmdev, Eknāth and Tukārām are also credited with Haripāṭh cycles; this id is Jñāneśvar's.

title: Hariścandra Kāvya (Rāghavāṅka)
summary: Rāghavāṅka's ṣaṭpadi retelling of King Hariścandra's trials for the sake of truth; a classic of the Vīraśaiva poets, though not a doctrinal Vīraśaiva work.

title: Hārīta Gītā

attribution.tradition: Bhīṣma, relating the rule of the mendicant (attributed in the vulgate to the sage Hārīta)
attribution.scholarly: a named teaching passage ('gītā') of the Mahābhārata

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa; the war and teaching at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages

scholarly.text: within the Mahābhārata's growth c. 4th c. BCE - 4th c. CE; the Śāntiparvan's Mokṣadharma belongs to the later layers

summary: The conduct by which the renunciant reaches Brahman: leaving home, equal in gain and loss, harming none in thought, word or look.
notes: The ascription to Hārīta is from the vulgate tradition; the critical text's opening was verified, the name was not.

queries: Gita Press vulgate colophons naming the gītā
checks.note: CE 12.269 (20 verses on the renunciant's conduct) confirmed. The critical text does not name Hārīta; the name comes from the vulgate colophon 'hārītagītāyām' (vulgate 12.278), as the unit's report said.

title: Hārīta Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: The tantra of Hārīta, disciple of Ātreya.
attribution.scholarly: The extant text is generally held to be a much later work bearing the old name.

summary: A medical compendium transmitted under the name of Ātreya's disciple Hārīta; the extant text is regarded by scholars as late.

title: Hārīta Dharmasūtra / Hārītasmṛti (fragments)
summary: An old Dharma text of Hārīta, lost and known from quotations (later metrical Laghu- and Vṛddha-Hārīta texts exist); it is often cited for the distinction between women who are 'speakers of Brahman' (brahmavādinī) and those who marry directly (sadyovadhū).
notes: The brahmavādinī/sadyovadhū quotation is known through later digests; wording not verified here.

queries: grep local smṛti collections for Hārīta
Harita dharmasutra brahmavadini sadyovadhu two kinds of women quoted Smriticandrika
checks.note: The later metrical Hārīta texts exist locally ('iti hārītasmṛtiḥ'; Vṛddha-Hārīta). The old Hārīta Dharmasūtra is known from quotations; Hindupedia describes Hārīta as an early Dharmasūtra author. The brahmavādinī/sadyovadhū quotation the entry names is confirmed as quoted in the Smṛticandrikā's saṃskāra section, per Wisdomlib's Medhātithi on MDh 2.66 (notes) and Wikipedia's Brahmavādinī article. The availability 'partly-lost' agrees.

title: Harivaṃśa
location_in_parent: Supplement (khila) appended to the Mahābhārata; critical edition in 118 chapters with appendices

attribution.tradition: Composed by Vyāsa as the khila of the Bhārata; recited by Vaiśampāyana to Janamejaya.
attribution.scholarly: A later supplement to the epic.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of the Dvāpara yuga

structure.description: Critical edition (BORI 1969–71) of about 118 chapters in three parts (Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu, Bhaviṣya parvans in the vulgate).

summary: The 'lineage of Hari', the supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata: the genealogy of the Vṛṣṇis, creation accounts, and the life of Kṛṣṇa from birth, including his youth among the cowherds of Vraja, to his deeds at Mathurā and Dvārakā.

editions.name: Harivaṃśa, Critical Edition, ed. P. L. Vaidya, BORI Pune (1969–1971)

queries: last verse number of the constituted text
checks.note: Extant and digitized. The locally held critical text ends at Hv 118.51, confirming the 118-chapter count that the entry gave from memory (its note can drop the low-confidence flag). Dates not independently checked beyond the entry's own "estimates vary".

Extant and digitized (DCS; GRETIL appendix; raw_etexts). Web: khila of the Mahābhārata; c. 1st-3rd c. CE; critical edition (P.L. Vaidya, 1969-71) of 118 chapters - itself also in three parvans (Harivaṃśa 1-45, Viṣṇu 46-113, Bhaviṣya 114-118).

notes: Chapter count of the critical text given from memory (low confidence).
alt_summary: Creation and the dynasties, then Kṛṣṇa's birth, childhood in Vraja (including the hallīsaka dance with the cowherd women), deeds at Mathurā and Dvārakā; the Purāṇic life of Kṛṣṇa that the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas expand.

title: Harivaṃśapurāṇa of Jinasena (Punnāṭa)
summary: The Punnāṭa monk Jinasena's purāṇa of the Hari lineage (783 CE): the life of the twenty-second Tīrthaṅkara Neminātha and of his cousin Kṛṣṇa (a vāsudeva) and Balarāma, the destruction of Dvārakā and the Pāṇḍavas' renunciation.

title: Harṣacarita

attribution.tradition: Bāṇabhaṭṭa
attribution.scholarly: Bāṇa, court poet of Harṣavardhana, 7th c.

summary: Bāṇa's account of Harṣa and his ancestors. Chapter 3 tells how king Puṣpabhūti, a devout Māheśvara, honoured Bhairavācārya, a great Śaiva from the south with thousands of disciples, and assisted him in a night rite in the great cremation ground.

editions.name: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) text

notes: Listed under the Kāpālikas because scholarship discusses Bhairavācārya among portraits of skull-and-cremation-ground Śaiva ascetics; the text itself calls him a great Śaiva (mahāśaiva), not a Kāpālika.

title: Hāsan Udās

attribution.tradition: the songs of Hāsan Rājā
attribution.scholarly: published 1907 (moderate confidence)

summary: Hāsan Rājā's songs of detachment from house and wealth and of the soul as a caged bird, in the Sylheti mystic-song idiom akin to the Bāuls'.

title: Hastāmalakīya (Hastāmalaka-stotra)
summary: Twelve (or fourteen) verses ascribed to Hastāmalaka, answering Śaṅkara's question 'who are you?' by declaring himself the eternal consciousness that, like the sun, illumines mind and senses; a commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.

title: Hastavālaprakaraṇa
summary: A short treatise with auto-commentary using the simile of a rope mistaken for a snake to show that conventional things, analysed into parts, are not found as they appear.

attribution.tradition: Āryadeva (Tibetan canon)
attribution.scholarly: ascribed to Dignāga in the Chinese; disputed

editions.name: Tibetan translation, Derge Tengyur D3844 (kārikā) — catalog:Derge-Tengyur:D3844
Tibetan translation, Derge Tengyur D3845 (vṛtti) — catalog:Derge-Tengyur:D3845

notes: Identification of D3844 with the Hastavāla to be checked; low confidence.

title: Hastyāyurveda
summary: The elephant medicine of Pālakāpya, framed as his dialogue with King Romapāda.

title: Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (Haṭhapradīpikā)

attribution.tradition: by Svātmārāma, who received haṭhavidyā through the grace of Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the Siddhas (1.4)
attribution.scholarly: compiled by Svātmārāma c. mid-15th c. from some twenty earlier texts (Amṛtasiddhi, DYŚ, Vivekamārtaṇḍa, Khecarīvidyā, Amaraughaprabodha, Amanaska and others)

tradition.text: in the succession of Ādinātha, Matsyendra and Gorakṣa

structure.description: vulgate: 4 upadeśas, c. 389 verses (āsana; prāṇāyāma and ṣaṭkarma; mudrā; samādhi/nādānusandhāna). A longer recension in 10 chapters is also transmitted.

summary: The classic compendium of haṭha, taught 'solely for rājayoga'. Upadeśa 1: lineage, secrecy, the hut, what destroys and promotes yoga, postures, diet. 2: breath-control, the purification of the channels, the six cleansing acts and the eight retentions, with warnings about improper practice. 3: kuṇḍalinī and the ten mudrās (including khecarī and vajrolī). 4: samādhi and its synonyms, the dissolution of mind and breath, śāmbhavī, the four stages and the inner sounds (nādānusandhāna), and the liberated yogin.

editions.name: The Haṭhayogapradīpikā with the Jyotsnā of Brahmānanda (Adyar Library 1893; 1972)
Haṭhapradīpikā, critical edition, Kaivalyadhama (Lonavla 1970; 10-chapter recension 1998)
GRETIL and sanskrit/raw_etexts e-texts

title: Jyotsnā (commentary on the Haṭhapradīpikā)

attribution.tradition: by Brahmānanda, pupil of Meruśāstrin
attribution.scholarly: 19th c. CE

structure.description: running commentary on all four upadeśas

summary: The standard Sanskrit commentary: it glosses haṭha as the union of 'ha' (sun, prāṇa) and 'ṭha' (moon, apāna), i.e. prāṇāyāma, and rājayoga as asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity; it discusses who is eligible (the dispassionate, per the Vāyu Saṃhitā, Sureśvara and Yājñavalkya), explains the practices, and reads the text through Pātañjala yoga and Advaita.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00243; Adyar Library edition

title: Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati

attribution.tradition: ascribed to Kapālakuruṇṭaka
attribution.scholarly: 18th c. CE; Maharashtra (recalled)

structure.description: prose sections on yamas and niyamas, cleansing, c. 112 postures, breath, mudrās and nāda

summary: A prose manual notable for describing more than a hundred postures, including many dynamic and rope postures not found in earlier texts, set within a sequence of yama, niyama, ṣaṭkarma, āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā and nāda.
notes: Known mainly through J. Birch's studies (recalled). Author name, count of postures and provenance low confidence.

title: Haṭharatnāvalī

attribution.tradition: by Śrīnivāsa (Śrīnivāsabhaṭṭa, 'mahāyogīndra')
attribution.scholarly: 17th c. CE; South Indian (Andhra?) author

structure.description: 4 upadeśas

summary: A haṭha manual that often argues with the Haṭhapradīpikā: it teaches eight cleansing acts (aṣṭakarma, adding cakrī and gajakaraṇī), the retentions and ten mudrās, names eighty-four postures and describes a selection, and treats the channels, centres, the inner sound and samādhi. It holds that mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja are one 'great yoga'.

editions.name: Haṭharatnāvalī of Śrīnivāsayogī, ed. M. L. Gharote, P. Devnath, V. K. Jha (Lonavla 2002)

notes: Contents recalled in outline; the Andhra provenance is a low-confidence recollection.

title: Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā

attribution.tradition: by Sundaradeva
attribution.scholarly: 18th c. CE; unpublished (manuscripts)

structure.description: not recalled

summary: Sundaradeva's second haṭha compendium, known from manuscripts; it collects postures, breath and mudrā teachings from earlier texts.
notes: Existence recalled from J. Birch's work on Sundaradeva; contents not recalled.

title: Haṭhatattvakaumudī

attribution.tradition: by Sundaradeva of Kāśī, son of Govindadeva, grandson of Viśvanāthadeva, of the Kāśyapa gotra (colophon)
attribution.scholarly: 18th c. CE

structure.description: 56 chapters (udyota) grouped in ullāsas, the last (9th) on rājayoga (Lonavla edition)

summary: A large compendium of haṭha that quotes and systematizes earlier texts: yamas and niyamas, the eight cleansing acts, postures, many retentions (including raising and lowering kinds), the three bandhas and mudrās, vajrolī, kuṇḍalinī and śakticālana, the channels and breaths, the sixteen supports, the centres, nāda, saguṇa and nirguṇa meditation, saṃyama and its powers, rājayoga, the signs of approaching death and the cheating of death.

editions.name: Haṭhatattvakaumudī of Sundaradeva, ed. M. L. Gharote, P. Devnath, V. K. Jha (Lonavla 2007)

notes: Chapter titles checked against the local eBhāratī e-text (colophons).

title: Hayagrīvastotra
summary: Deśika's hymn to Hayagrīva, the horse-headed form of the Lord as the giver of knowledge.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

summary: Śiva teaches the Self as one pure consciousness distinct from body and mind, the Sāṃkhya categories under the Lord, his own supremacy (displayed in a cosmic dance), devotion and knowledge, and an eight-limbed yoga ending in the Pāśupata yoga of smearing with sacred ash and meditating on Īśāna as the supreme light, which frees the bound soul (paśu) from its bonds (pāśa).

title: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā
summary: Utpaladeva's verse exposition of the 'recognition of the Lord': in the section on knowledge he answers the Buddhist logician's denial of an enduring self (1.2) and shows that cognition, memory and exclusion require one conscious subject (1.3-1.4) whose essence is reflexive awareness (1.5); the section on action shows action and relation to be the Lord's; the section on scripture sets out the tattvas, the pramātṛs and the three malas (3.1-3.2); the summary section (4) closes with the simile of the unrecognized lover (4.17).

title: Jaimini Upadeśa Sūtras
summary: A sūtra text in four adhyāyas of four pādas on the Jaimini system of horā: aspects by sign (rāśi-dṛṣṭi), the variable significators (cara-kāraka) headed by the ātmakāraka, the kārakāṃśa, ārūḍha and upapada, sign-based periods such as the cara-daśā, and longevity. Numbers and signs are encoded by the kaṭapayādi system. It names the signs in the chart that indicate liberation (kaivalya).

summary: One of the three gems of the Pāñcarātra, in 33 paṭalas. Sages ask Śāṇḍilya, who relates Bhagavān's teaching to Nārada. title: Kālāma Sutta
summary: To the Kālāmas of Kesaputta, perplexed by rival teachers: do not go by oral tradition, lineage, report, scripture, logic, inference, reasoned reflection, acceptance of a view, a speaker's competence or respect for one's teacher; when you know for yourselves that things are unwholesome and lead to harm, abandon them; the four assurances of one whose mind is free of enmity.

title: Kālikā Purāṇa
summary: For the Bengal–Assam lineage: the Upapurāṇa of Kāmarūpa, telling Satī's death, Śiva's grief and the scattering of her body into the pīṭhas (feet at Devīkūṭa, thighs at Uḍḍīyāna, yoni at Kāmagiri in Kāmarūpa, breasts at Jālandhara, shoulders and neck at Pūrṇagiri) (ch. 18 in the Vaṅgavāsī ed.); the worship of Kāmākhyā and of Tripurā; and the chapter on offerings (the 'rudhirādhyāya', ch. 67 in that edition), with its substitutes and prohibitions (summary only).

The Olivelle dating is confirmed at group level (Wikipedia, Sannyasa Upanishads). Seven older texts reach their final form between the last centuries BCE and c. 300 CE. The Āśrama is 3rd c. CE, the Nāradaparivrājaka and Śāṭyāyanīya c. 12th c., and about ten others 14th-15th c. The tradition account (śruti, authorless) is left as it is.

summary: No. 27 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Devavibhava (Kiraṇa: Devapitṛ), then the sage Saṃvartaka. The Kāmika assigns it 9 upabheda(s): Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Nīla, Rūkṣa, Bhānuka, Dhenuka, Prabuddha, Buddha, Kāla. A dialogue in which Garuḍa questions Śiva. title: Kubjikāmata Tantra
summary: The root scripture of the Kubjikā cult (the Kulālikāmnāya recension), a dialogue of Bhairava and the Goddess: her descent at Candradvīpa and emergence from the liṅga as the bent Kubjikā, her journey through the sacred seats and the founding of the 'western' transmission (1-2); the Mālinī and mantra system (3-10); the six centres with their deities and yoginīs (11-16); the haṃsa and the fourfold order (17-19); the island-transmission (20-21); knowledge of the three times and yogic departure (23); worship (24); the observance (25).

queries: Laghu Yoga Vasistha Gauda Abhinanda 6000 verses date
checks.note: Confirmed: extant and local (Nirṇaya Sāgara 1933 with the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā; eBhārati). It has six prakaraṇas (3 + 1 + 9 + 5 + 10 + 18 sargas), the closing verse lists the six, and it runs to about 6,000 verses. The final colophon ascribes it to 'gauḍamaṇḍalālaṅkāra śrīmad-abhinanda'. Some colophons call it 'yogavāsiṣṭhasāra', which supports that alt title. Not settled: Slaje argues that the Kashmiri Abhinanda (Jayanta's son) and the Gauḍa Abhinanda of that colophon are distinct, so a 10th-c. date is untenable. The entry's c. 10th-11th c. stays low confidence. Availability is digitized-original.

title: Lakṣmīdharā (commentary on the Saundaryalaharī)

scholarly.text: c. early 16th c. CE (associated with the court of the Gajapati Pratāparudra of Orissa)

title: Lalitā Sahasranāma
summary: The thousand names of Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī, framed as Hayagrīva's teaching to Agastya. The names describe her form and weapons, her city and palace, her war on Bhaṇḍāsura, her subtle body as the three sections of the Śrīvidyā mantra, her ascent as kuṇḍalinī through the cakras and knots, her qualityless nature, the three states and the fourth, the five cosmic acts, the Śrīcakra and her oneness with Śiva. Recitation and worship with the names are central Śākta practices.
location_in_parent: said to be in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, in the Hayagrīva-Agastya dialogue (colophon)

attribution.tradition: Composed at Lalitā's command by the eight goddesses of speech (Vaśinī and the others), who knew the secret of her cakra; named the 'Rahasya-nāma-sāhasra'; taught by Hayagrīva to Agastya (pūrvabhāga 32-33 in Bhāskararāya's numbering).
attribution.scholarly: Not part of the main printed Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa; a Śrīvidyā composition of uncertain date, authoritative by the time of Bhāskararāya (18th c.).

structure.description: An introductory part (pūrvabhāga, 51 verses in Bhāskararāya's count), the thousand names in 182½ anuṣṭubh verses with no name repeated and no filler particles, and a concluding part (phalaśruti); 320 verses in all by Bhāskararāya's count. The stotra proper is usually numbered 1-183.

title: Mahābhārata

attribution.tradition: Composed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, taught to his disciples, recited by Vaiśampāyana at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and retold by Ugraśravas Sauti to the sages of Naimiṣa forest at Śaunaka's twelve-year sacrifice.
attribution.scholarly: A composite work of many hands grown over several centuries around a narrative core; the frame narratives and the didactic books (esp. Śānti and Anuśāsana) are generally held to be later layers.

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: composed and expanded in stages, c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

structure.description: 18 books (parvans), traditionally 100 sub-books (upaparvans) as listed in the Parvasaṃgraha (1.2); the Harivaṃśa is its supplement (khila). The tradition speaks of 100,000 verses (śatasāhasrī saṃhitā); 1.1.61 says Vyāsa made a 24,000-verse Bhārata without the sub-stories (upākhyānas); 1.1.50 records three starting points used by reciters (Manu, Āstīka, Uparicara). The critical text as digitized locally has 2,097 chapters and about 73,800 verse units.

summary: The great epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, calling itself a 'fifth Veda' (kārṣṇa veda) and a treatise on dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; besides the narrative it contains extended teaching sections (the Bhagavad Gītā, the Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma of the Śāntiparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, the Nārāyaṇīya). It says of itself that what is found here on the four aims of life is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere (1.56.33).

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a verse work in thirty-two chapters: the first sets out the purport of all scripture (Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences, the gradation of souls, bhakti as the means); the second the principles of interpretation, including the threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata; the third creation; and the rest retell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, including Kṛṣṇa's life, in the light of that purport. It closes with the author naming himself the third form of Vāyu, born when 4,300 years of Kali had passed.

title: Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya
summary: Patañjali's 'great commentary' on Pāṇini's sūtras and Kātyāyana's vārttikas, in lively dialogue. Its introduction (Paspaśā) asks what a word is, gives the purposes of studying grammar — protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, the scriptural command, brevity and certainty — tells how Bṛhaspati taught Indra words one by one for a thousand divine years without reaching the end, reads the Ṛgveda's 'four horns' verse as a praise of grammar, and holds that the Asuras were defeated for mispronouncing speech.

scholarly.text: c. mid-2nd c. BCE (the text refers to sacrificing for Puṣyamitra)

structure.description: 85 āhnikas ('daily lessons'), the first being the Paspaśā

editions.name: Kielhorn's edition via GRETIL (local Devanāgarī mirror)

checks.note: Extant. All Paspaśā passages cited in the summary are text-located. The mid-2nd c. BCE date (Puṣyamitra) is the standard scholarly dating (see tch:patanjali-grammarian). The '85 āhnikas' count was not re-counted.

alt_summary: U31 contribution: for the grammarian-philosophers the Mahābhāṣya supplies the founding questions — what the word is (the Paspaśā's answer: that by whose utterance the thing is understood), the eternity of word, meaning and relation (Kātyāyana's first vārttika), the sphoṭa as the word with sound (dhvani) as its quality (on P 1.1.70), and whether words denote the universal or the individual (Vājapyāyana and Vyāḍi, on P 1.2.64).

U33 contribution: in the discussion under Pāṇini 2.4.12 Patañjali gives 'śramaṇabrāhmaṇam' as the example of a dvandva of beings 'whose enmity is perpetual' (P 2.4.9), alongside crow-and-owl and dog-and-jackal.

title: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra
summary: The Buddha's final Mahāyāna teaching on the day of his parinirvāṇa: the Tathāgata is permanent and unchanging; his parinirvāṇa is a skillful display; nirvāṇa has permanence, bliss, self and purity; 'self' means the tathāgatagarbha; all sentient beings have buddha-nature, obscured by defilements; buddha-nature is the emptiness of the highest meaning, wisdom, the middle way. The early part (Faxian's 6-fascicle version) excludes the icchantika; the later part (Dharmakṣema's 40-fascicle version, Lion's Roar and Kāśyapa chapters) affirms that icchantikas too have buddha-nature. It forbids eating meat.

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. checks.note: 12 prose sections confirmed. The note that Madhva's school treats the first chapter (Āgama-prakaraṇa) of the Kārikā as śruti fits Wikipedia's Gauḍapāda article: Rāmānuja and Madhva regarded its first chapter as śruti, while Advaita scholars did not. Scholarly dating fits Olivelle's chronology as reported on the web: BĀU and ChU pre-Buddhist, 7th–6th c. BCE; TU, AU and KauU probably pre-Buddhist, 6th–5th c. BCE; the verse Upaniṣads (Kena oldest, then Kaṭha, Īśa, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka) in the last few centuries BCE; Praśna and Māṇḍūkya not much older than the start of the common era. summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, reading it as teaching Viṣṇu's supremacy and his difference from souls and matter, often by etymological explanation of names and by quotations from other scriptures. Madhva's text of the Upaniṣad includes the verses that Advaita attributes to Gauḍapāda's Kārikā (read by him as śruti); he explains Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña and Turīya as four forms of Viṣṇu, and the tradition's account of its origin is Varuṇa, as a frog, praising the fourfold Nārāyaṇa.

summary: Dolpopa's principal treatise on other-emptiness, written as final, uncommon instructions for mountain retreatants. It sets out buddha-nature (the matrix of the one gone thus) as the ultimate that is empty of all adventitious, conventional phenomena but not of its own nature, permanent and endowed with the buddha-qualities; distinguishes self-emptiness of the conventional from other-emptiness of the ultimate; and supports this with extensive citation of the tathāgatagarbha sūtras, the Maitreya texts, Nāgārjuna's hymns and the Kālacakra literature.

Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. summary: Anuruddha's verse manual on the delimitation of mind and matter, a second Abhidhamma primer by the author of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

title: Namaskāra-mantra (Navakāra, Pañca-parameṣṭhi-namaskāra)
alt_titles: Pañcamaṅgala-mahāśrutaskandha (Śvetāmbara name for the mantra with cūlikā)

attribution.tradition: eternal (anādi); no author
attribution.scholarly: the five homages appear at the opening of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Bhagavatī; an early form of the first homages occurs in Khāravela's Hāthīgumphā inscription

title: Nāmdev Gāthā

attribution.tradition: Nāmdev's; he vowed to compose a hundred crore abhaṅgas and his household (Janābāī) completed them.
attribution.scholarly: A large corpus with layers; several later Nāmdevs (e.g. Viṣṇudās Nāmā) may be mixed in.

tradition.text: Nāmdev 1270–1350

title: Dorje Sempa Namkha Che (rdo rje sems dpa' nam mkha' che, Vajrasattva, Great Space)
summary: A root scripture of the mind series ('great space'), often paired with the Kunjed Gyalpo; it exists in several versions and is quoted by Longchenpa.
notes: From memory; versions and chapter structure not recorded.

title: Ornament of the Essence of Explanation (rnam bshad snying po'i rgyan)
summary: Gyaltsab Je's commentary on the Abhisamayālaṅkāra with Haribhadra.

editions.name: Tibetan: collected works (gsung 'bum), several xylograph and modern editions

title: Nānātitthiyasāvaka Sutta
summary: Deities who had been disciples of rival teachers praise Pūraṇa, Makkhali, the Nigaṇṭha and Pakudha in verse; Māra, possessing one of them, praises austerity and heaven; the Buddha exposes him.
notes: Section numbers follow SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation; checked against the local e-text.

title: Nandakovāda Sutta
summary: Nandaka's instruction to Mahāpajāpatī's five hundred nuns on the impermanence of the senses; all attain at least stream-entry.

title: Nandī Sūtra

title: Nandikeśvara-kāśikā
summary: U31 contribution: the verse commentary reading the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras (the phoneme list sounded by Śiva's drum) as teachings on the supreme and its manifestation — the letter a as the supreme Lord and the sounds as the unfolding of Śiva and Śakti; a bridge between grammar and mantra theory.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed. It reads the sūtras metaphysically ('akāro brahmarūpaḥ …'), as the entry says. The date remains unverified.

alt_summary: A short verse commentary ascribed to Nandikeśvara that reads the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras as teachings on the supreme reality and its manifestation; it opens with the story that at the end of his dance Śiva, the king of dancers, sounded his drum fourteen times to uplift Sanaka and the other perfected sages.
notes: Date and verse numbers not verified; the opening story is widely quoted.

title: Nangjang (snang sbyang, Refining Apparent Phenomena)
summary: Dudjom Lingpa's visionary Dzogchen treatise in dialogue form on the ground, delusion, and the view.

title: Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan
alt_titles: A Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the Southern Seas
summary: Yijing's account of Indian monastic practice according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, describing four principal nikāyas — Mahāsāṃghika, Sthavira, Mūlasarvāstivāda and Saṃmitīya — and their regional distribution.

title: Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti
summary: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār's 96 veṇpās, opening 'Nārāyaṇa created the four-faced one' — a sustained assertion of Nārāyaṇa's supremacy over Brahmā and Śiva and of refuge in him alone.

tradition.text: close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

title: Naṉṉūl

title: Nañvāda
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's treatise on the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

title: Miscellaneous Dialogues of the Reverend of Nanyang (Shenhui)

notes: Dunhuang manuscripts (ed. Hu Shi); not held locally. The four-phrase characterisation of Northern practice (凝心入定，住心看淨，起心外照，攝心內證) is quoted from memory — moderate confidence.

title: Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
summary: Eighty-four aphorisms attributed to the sage Nārada defining devotion as supreme love (parama-prema) of the nature of nectar, 'the fruit itself', higher than action, knowledge and yoga; they give earlier teachers' definitions and the gopīs as the model, the means (renunciation, unceasing worship, hearing and singing, above all the grace of great souls), the things to avoid, the signs of the lover of God, the eleven forms of attachment, and the line of bhakti teachers.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by the divine sage Nārada ('nārada-proktam', NBS 84).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; usually dated after the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, c. 10th–13th c. CE or later.

summary: A Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa of dharma and ritual: devotion to Viṣṇu, the Vedāṅgas, mantra-śāstra, the tithi-vratas of the year, the contents of all eighteen Purāṇas, the Ekādaśī vow (with Yama's lament that his realm is emptied by it), and the glories of many tīrthas.

title: Nāradasmṛti

title: Nāradīya Śikṣā
summary: The phonetic manual of the Sāmaveda: it names the seven sāman notes and sets them against the notes of the flute (1.5.1–2: the first of the Sāman singers is the flute's madhyama, the second gāndhāra, the third ṛṣabha, the fourth ṣaḍja, the fifth dhaivata, the sixth niṣāda, the seventh pañcama), gives the places of the notes in the body and on the fingers (1.7), and teaches the gestures and faults of chanting.

checks.note: Extant; structure 2 prapāṭhakas × 8 kaṇḍikās confirmed in the local text; the note-mapping of 1.5.1–2 and the places of notes in 1.7 confirmed. Ascription to Nārada is the text's own tradition; no date given in the entry.
Extant locally under the Sāmaveda Śikṣās. Its content on svaras, grāmas and mūrchanās is standard.

alt_summary: The Śikṣā of the Sāmaveda: it relates the Vedic accents and the tones of sāman chanting to the seven musical notes (svara) beginning with ṣaḍja, and treats the grāmas, mūrchanās and the manner of singing — a bridge between Vedic phonetics and the later science of music.

U31 contribution: the Sāmaveda's phonetic manual is also the oldest source of the music tradition's notes — it sets the seven Sāman notes against the flute's notes (1.5.1–2), gives the animal cries of the notes (1.5.3–4), the grāmas and mūrchanās, and the places of the notes in the body.

title: Nirukta
summary: Yāska's explanation of the Nighaṇṭu and of Vedic words. Book 1 sets out the four classes of words (1.1), Vārṣyāyaṇi's six modifications of being (1.2), the dispute whether all nouns come from verbs (1.12–14), Kautsa's claim that mantras are meaningless and its refutation (1.15–16), praise of understanding (1.18) and the origin of the Veda and Vedāṅgas from the seers' direct vision (1.20); book 2 gives the rules of etymology (2.1) and of teaching (2.3–4) and defines the seer as the one who saw (2.11); books 7–12 explain the deities as three, of one self praised in many ways (7.4–5).

summary: The chief Chedasūtra: in twenty sections it lists the transgressions of monks and nuns and the atonement (prāyaścitta) fixed for each. summary: The earliest surviving Śaiva tantra and No. 12 (Rudrabheda) of the 28 Siddhānta scriptures. summary: Vātsyāyana's commentary, the oldest extant on the Nyāya Sūtra. It explains that a means of knowledge is purposeful because it makes action successful, defines nyāya as the examination of things by the means of knowledge, presents ānvīkṣikī as the fourth science distinct from the Upaniṣadic science of the self, reads the five members as a convergence of all four means of knowledge, catalogues the forms of false knowledge, rejects eternal pleasure in liberation, describes Īśvara as a distinct self who assists human effort, and prescribes yama, niyama, yoga and contemplation of the unlovely against passion.

It presents reasoning about the Lord as a form of worship and opens with a passage on the names under which the schools worship Him.

summary: The root text of Nyāya. It opens by promising the highest good (niḥśreyasa) from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), states the chain from false knowledge to liberation (1.1.2), defines the four means of knowledge, the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self, the five-membered demonstration, debate, pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat (book 1); examines the means of knowledge (book 2), the self, body, senses, cognition and mind (book 3), faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation, the whole and atoms, rival views such as momentariness and idealism, and the yogic means to knowledge of truth (book 4); and lists the twenty-four futile rejoinders and twenty-two points of defeat (book 5).

alt_summary: U33 contribution: Jayanta reports three grades of Cārvāka — the old Cārvāka teachers who held consciousness of the elements; the 'rogue Cārvāka' (cārvāka-dhūrta) who, promising to explain the principles, explained only that the number and definitions of the means of knowledge cannot be fixed; and the 'well-educated Cārvākas' (suśikṣita-cārvāka) who accept a single knower lasting as long as the body but deny that it survives the body.

title: Nyāyāmṛta

structure.description: 4 paricchedas

summary: Vyāsatīrtha's great polemic against Advaita, in four chapters that follow the four chapters of the Brahmasūtras: (1) the reality of the world — a refutation of the five Advaita definitions of falsity (mithyātva) and of the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness; (2) the Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite, attributeless meaning, and the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; (3) the means — against the Vivaraṇa view of hearing, reflection and meditation, the Lord is to be won by direct realization born of meditation; (4) liberation is not the mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated, from Brahmā and Rudra down, are graded. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it point by point.

summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's Advaita commentary on the adhikaraṇas of the first pāda(s) of the Brahma Sūtras.

title: Nyāyaratna
summary: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra's pre-Gaṅgeśa work on inference and related topics, regarded as a forerunner of Navya-Nyāya.
notes: Low confidence on title details; listed as a gap to check.

title: Nyāyaratnākara
