title: Nyāyaratnamālā
summary: Pārthasārathi Miśra's independent treatise on selected Mīmāṃsā topics (e.g. the validity of cognition, injunction).

title: Nyāyaratnāvalī (Padmanābha Tīrtha)
summary: Padmanābha Tīrtha's commentary on the Anuvyākhyāna, preceding Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā.
notes: Disambiguated from Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Advaita Nyāyaratnāvalī (on the Siddhāntabindu). Title recalled, not verified.

title: Nyāyasāra

summary: Bhāsarvajña's manual in three chapters (perception, inference, verbal testimony): it accepts only three means of knowledge, treats yogic perception, and holds — against the mainstream — that liberation is the absolute cessation of pain together with the experience of eternal bliss; its last part links the path to Śaiva yoga.

title: Nyāyasiddhāñjana
summary: Deśika's treatise on the categories of Viśiṣṭādvaita — insentient substance, soul, Lord, the eternal realm, cognition and non-substances.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa
summary: Śaśadhara's pre-Gaṅgeśa treatise on Nyāya topics.

title: Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Viśvanātha's auto-commentary on the Bhāṣāpariccheda, the standard intermediate text of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika in Navya-Nyāya idiom (e.g. its inference of a maker from the effecthood of earth, sprouts and the like).

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's index of the sūtras and prakaraṇas of the Nyāya Sūtra, which fixed the sūtra text as read by the later tradition; its closing verse gives a date (year 898 of an unnamed era).

title: Nyāyasudhā
summary: Jayatīrtha's great commentary on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna, the most authoritative exposition of Dvaita doctrine and polemic, esteemed in the tradition as its central scholastic text; it expands Madhva's arguments against Advaita, Buddhist, Jain, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya positions.

title: Nyāyasudhā-parimala

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's commentary on Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, from which he is called Parimalācārya.

title: Nyāyasudhā (Rāṇaka)
notes: Distinct from Jayatīrtha's Dvaita Nyāyasudhā (src:nyayasudha).
summary: Someśvara Bhaṭṭa's commentary on Kumārila's Tantravārttika, known as Rāṇaka.

title: Nyāyasūtravṛtti (Viśvanātha)

scholarly.text: 1634 CE (date given in the text, as usually reported)

summary: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana's running commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra, in Navya-Nyāya idiom.

title: Nyāyatattva
summary: Nāthamuni's lost work on logic and the means of knowledge, which later Viśiṣṭādvaita logicians (Vedānta Deśika's Nyāyapariśuddhi) say they follow; known only from citations.

tradition.text: Nāthamuni, traditionally 9th–10th c. (hagiographies give an extremely long life)

title: Nyāyāvatāra

attribution.tradition: Siddhasena Divākara
attribution.scholarly: attribution debated: several scholars ascribe it to a later Siddhasena (Mahāmati) writing after Dharmakīrti

scholarly.text: 5th c. if by Siddhasena Divākara; c. 6th–8th c. if later

summary: A 32-verse manual of Jain logic: valid cognition (pramāṇa) as knowledge illuminating itself and its object without contradiction, perception and inference for oneself and for others, the fallacies, and the place of the standpoints.

title: Nyāyaviniścaya
summary: Akalaṅka's treatise on perception, inference and scripture, written largely against Dharmakīrti.

title: Nyāyavivaraṇa

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a short prose work setting out, adhikaraṇa by adhikaraṇa, the reasoning (nyāya) by which Madhva reads the Brahmasūtras.

title: Nyida Khajor (nyi zla kha sbyor, the Union of Sun and Moon)
summary: One of the Seventeen Tantras; known for its teaching on the bardos.
notes: Not local. Membership of the Seventeen from memory; content summary minimal.

title: Nyingma Gyubum (rnying ma rgyud 'bum, the Collected Tantras of the Ancients)
summary: The canon of Old Tantras not (or only partly) admitted to the Kangyur: the tantras of Atiyoga (mind, space and instruction series, incl. the Seventeen Tantras), Anuyoga (the root sūtras) and Mahāyoga (tantra section and sādhana section), with protector texts. Compiled in its extant form from the 15th c.

attribution.tradition: The tantras were taught by the buddhas of the three kāyas and translated in the first diffusion; Ratna Lingpa (1403-1479) gathered them into a collection.
attribution.scholarly: Several editions (Tingkye, Tsamdrag, Derge, Kathmandu) differ in contents and order; the Derge edition was prepared under Getse Paṇḍita in the late 18th c.

tradition.text: taught beyond time; translated 8th-10th c.

structure.description: Arranged by vehicle: Atiyoga, Anuyoga, Mahāyoga; editions of c. 25-46 volumes (exact counts differ by edition; not recorded here)

notes: Not local. Volume counts omitted deliberately (see REPORT.md).

title: Nyingma Kama (rnying ma bka' ma, the Canonical Transmission)
summary: The collection of the 'spoken word' lineage of the Nyingma: the three inner tantras with their commentaries, empowerment and sādhana texts transmitted without interruption from the first diffusion (as distinct from treasures). Edited at Mindroling by Terdak Lingpa and Lochen Dharmaśrī, and greatly expanded by Dudjom Rinpoche in the 20th c.

title: De bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po bstan pa (Rangjung Dorje's Treatise on Buddha-Nature)
summary: The Third Karmapa's short verse treatise on buddha-nature: the ground is mind's nature, luminous and empty, obscured by adventitious stains; purification is Mahāmudrā.

attribution.tradition: Karmapa Rangjung Dorje
attribution.scholarly: Rangjung Dorje (1284-1339)

title: Nyingthig Yabzhi (snying thig ya bzhi, the Four Parts of the Heart-essence)
summary: Longchenpa's compilation of the instruction-series Heart-essence: the Vima Nyingthig with his Lama Yangtig, and the Khandro Nyingthig with his Khandro Yangtig, completed by his Zabmo Yangtig.

title: Pure Rules of Ōbaku (Ōbaku shingi)
summary: Ōbaku monastic code (1672) compiled under Ingen, with Ming-style ordination, chanting and ritual.

title: Mahāmudrā: The Ocean of Definitive Meaning

summary: The 9th Karmapa's large Mahāmudrā manual: the common, uncommon and special preliminaries; śamatha; vipaśyanā; the pointing-out of mind; enhancement and removal of obstacles; the four yogas; the fruition.

summary: Genshin's anthology of scripture on birth in Sukhāvatī, beginning with vivid accounts of the hells and the six paths to be loathed and the ten pleasures of the Pure Land to be sought; its core is contemplative and oral nenbutsu arranged by Vasubandhu's five gates, with the famous rules for the dying; sent to China and deeply influential in Japan.

notes: Text not in the local corpus; chapter structure and teachings recalled.

title: Embossed Tea Kettle (Orategama)
summary: Hakuin's letters (1749–1751) to a feudal lord and others: the importance of practice in the midst of activity over quiet sitting, the naikan method, and nenbutsu and kōan.

title: Oṣadhi Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.97)
summary: The physician's hymn to the healing plants, born three ages before the gods; where plants gather like kings in assembly, that inspired one is called a physician, slayer of demons and dispeller of disease.

title: Ösel Nyingpo (gsang snying spyi don 'od gsal snying po, the Essence of Clear Light)
summary: Mipham's general exposition of the Guhyagarbha: the view of great purity and equality, the 'superior two truths', and the path of Mahāyoga.

title: Oupnek'hat
summary: Anquetil-Duperron's Latin rendering (1801–1802) of the Persian Sirr-i Akbar; the first Upaniṣad collection widely read in Europe.

title: Pacalāyamāna Sutta
summary: Advice to the drowsy Moggallāna: eight remedies for drowsiness, and not to go among families with the banner of conceit raised; 'nothing is worth clinging to'.

title: Padaratnāvalī
summary: Vijayadhvaja Tīrtha's word-by-word commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the standard Mādhva commentary on it.

title: Padārthādarśa of Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka, finished in Vārāṇasī in 1493/94, which quotes a very wide range of Āgamas, Tantras and Purāṇas; among them the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā's definitions of spoken, whispered and mental japa.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).
alt_summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary on the Śāradātilaka, rich in quotations from lost tantras.

title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
summary: Praśastapāda's systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (often called Praśastapādabhāṣya, though not a line-by-line commentary): after saluting Īśvara and Kaṇāda it declares knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the six categories the cause of the highest good, arising from dharma manifested by the Lord's command; it fixes twenty-four qualities, gives the account of cosmic dissolution and creation by Maheśvara's will, divides cognition into knowledge (perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge) and its opposites, treats yogic perception, dharma and adharma, and liberation.
notes: Commentaries: Vyomaśiva's Vyomavatī, Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī, Udayana's Kiraṇāvalī, and later ones.

title: Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's critical re-examination of the Vaiśeṣika list of categories, proposing reductions and additions to the traditional seven.
notes: The specific revisions (e.g. treatment of space, time and ultimate particularity) are recalled with low confidence and are not asserted as teachings in this skeleton.

title: Padma Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Compiled by Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana) from the one primeval Purāṇa and taught through Romaharṣaṇa and his line. Told of the time when the world was a golden lotus (Matsya 53.14).
attribution.scholarly: Survives in two main recensions - a Bengal recension in five khaṇḍas (Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga, Pātāla, Uttara) and a western Indian recension in six khaṇḍas, the one printed (Ānandāśrama) and usually studied (the Venkateshwara print arranges Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga, Brahma, Pātāla, Uttara and Kriyāyogasāra); many layers of different date.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: layered compilation; estimates range from c. 4th to 15th c. CE, some parts c. 750-1000 CE

structure.description: khaṇḍas differing by recension; 55,000 verses by the traditional count (BhP 12.13.4; Matsya 53.14)

notes: Contains the Bhāgavata-māhātmya (Uttarakhaṇḍa; colophon checked in the local e-text), the Gītā-māhātmya, the Śiva Gītā (U06), the classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas (Uttarakhaṇḍa; ch. number edition-dependent, often cited as 236.18-21), and the list of ten offences against the name as cited by Gauḍīya authors.
summary: A vast Vaiṣṇava-leaning compendium: creation, tīrthas (Puṣkara and others), vratas (Ekādaśī, Kārttika, Māgha), the glory of the Bhāgavata and the Gītā, Rāma narratives, the worship of the name and of the śālagrāma and tulasī, and the guṇa-classification of the eighteen Purāṇas.

title: Pādma Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: revealed by Bhagavān (Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva); one of the traditional 108 saṃhitās

structure.description: jñānapāda, yogapāda, kriyāpāda, caryāpāda

editions.name: Pādma Saṃhitā, Pāñcarātra Pariśodhana Pariṣad, Madras (caryāpāda 1974; other pādas 1982)

notes: eBhāratī e-text consulted locally (padmasaMhitA.md).
summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā in the four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), presented as the expansion of the Jayākhya and followed in practice at Hastiśaila (Kāñcī). title: Padmapurāṇa of Raviṣeṇa

title: Pādukāsahasra
summary: Deśika's 1,008 verses in 32 sections (paddhati) on the sandals of Raṅganātha, composed, the tradition says, in a single night; the sandals are Nammāḻvār (Śaṭhakopa) and the teacher who carries the Lord to the devotee.

title: Padyāvalī
summary: Rūpa's anthology of devotional verses by many poets, including the verses later gathered as Caitanya's Śikṣāṣṭaka.

summary: Rāmasiṃha's Apabhraṃśa dohās criticising outer religion — pilgrimage, temple and image — and locating the Jina in the temple of the body; close in idiom to the Buddhist and later Sant dohās.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पाहुड-दोहा--राम-सिंह-मुनि); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

title: Paiṅgala Upaniṣad

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

title: Paitāmaha Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta ascribed to Pitāmaha (Brahmā); its early form, close to the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, is summarized in the Pañcasiddhāntikā; a later form is preserved in the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa and underlies Brahmagupta's work.
notes: Known chiefly through Varāhamihira's Pañcasiddhāntikā.

attribution.tradition: by Mahārāj Viśvanāth Siṃh of Rewā
attribution.scholarly: 19th c.; reads Kabīr's Rām in a Rāma-bhakti sense

summary: A royal commentary on the Bījak, 'the destroyer of hypocrisy', which reads Kabīr's critique of outward religion within a Vaiṣṇava Rāma-bhakti frame.

title: Paḻamoḻi Nāṉūṟu
summary: Four hundred quatrains each ending in a proverb (paḻamoḻi), by the Jain poet Muṉṟuṟai Araiyaṉār; one of the Eighteen Minor Classics.

title: Tipiṭaka (the Pali Canon)
summary: The three 'baskets' of the Theravāda canon — Vinaya (monastic discipline), Sutta (discourses) and Abhidhamma (analysis of phenomena) — held to be the word of the Buddha as rehearsed at the First Council and transmitted orally until written down in Sri Lanka.

structure.description: Vinaya Piṭaka (Suttavibhaṅga, Khandhaka, Parivāra); Sutta Piṭaka (Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara and Khuddaka Nikāyas); Abhidhamma Piṭaka (seven books: Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, Paṭṭhāna)

tradition.text: rehearsed at the First Council at Rājagaha in the first rains after the parinibbāna (543 BCE by the Theravāda reckoning); written down on palm leaves at the Āloka-vihāra (Aluvihāra), Sri Lanka, under King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya

scholarly.text: oral composition and redaction c. 5th–1st c. BCE; first written c. 29–17 BCE (Vaṭṭagāmaṇī); later KN books and the Abhidhamma the latest strata

title: Pāmpāṭṭic cittar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of the snake-charmer Siddhar)
summary: Songs with the refrain 'āṭu pāmpē' ('dance, O snake!'), addressed to the snake: praise of Śiva and the guru, the impermanence and filth of the body, the uselessness of learning, caste and ritual for liberation, and the inner ascent. Later readers take the snake as the coiled power (kuṇṭali) within.

scholarly.text: undetermined; the Siddhar song corpus is usually placed c. 1400–1800

summary: Paippalāda asks the Lord what arose first; Maheśa answers with the five faces of Śiva (Sadyojāta, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna) and their correspondences; later verses, addressed to Śākala, teach the five-syllable mantra and Śiva in the cave of the heart.

title: Pañcadaśī

attribution.tradition: Vidyāraṇya; some accounts ascribe part of the work to Bhāratītīrtha
attribution.scholarly: Vidyāraṇya (with possible co-authorship)

structure.description: 15 chapters in three groups of five

summary: Vidyāraṇya's fifteen-chapter verse manual in three pentads — five 'discriminations' (viveka: of reality, the elements, the sheaths, duality, the great sayings), five 'lamps' (dīpa: the picture, contentment, the immutable, meditation, the theatre) and five 'blisses' (ānanda: of yoga, of the self, of non-duality, of knowledge, of objects). It distinguishes māyā (pure sattva) as the adjunct of Īśvara from avidyā (impure sattva) as the adjunct of the jīva, and gives the canvas, four-space, tenth-man and theatre-lamp illustrations and the seven states of the jīva.

title: Pañcādhyāyī
summary: Pāṇḍe Rājamalla's unfinished Sanskrit treatise on substance and on right view, organised by the standpoints; an important text of the Adhyātma current.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:पंचाध्यायी); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date. (catalogue gives no author).

title: Pañcakalpa
summary: A Chedasūtra on monastic conduct counted in some old lists (instead of the Jītakalpa); the root text is lost, and only a bhāṣya and cūrṇi material are known (low confidence).

title: Pañcakrama

attribution.tradition: by Nāgārjuna (identified with the Madhyamaka master)
attribution.scholarly: by a tantric Nāgārjuna c. 9th–10th c.; some chapters attributed by later tradition to other members of the school

structure.description: 5 chapters (krama)

summary: The 'Five Stages' of the Ārya school: vajra recitation, the purification of all (the four empties and the natural concepts), self-consecration (illusory body), full awakening (clear light) and union (yuganaddha); the text states that the stages are 'a staircase' for those established in the generation stage.

title: Pañcapādikā

attribution.tradition: Padmapāda; the name 'five pādas' and the tradition that the rest was destroyed (his uncle burnt the manuscript, Śaṅkaradigvijaya) explain why only the opening survives
attribution.scholarly: Padmapāda (8th c.)

summary: Padmapāda's commentary on the adhyāsa-bhāṣya and the first four sūtras of Śaṅkara's BSBh: analyses the definition of superimposition, presents ignorance as an insentient power (avidyā-śakti) that is the material cause of superimposition, glosses 'mithyā' as 'indescribable', and treats the jīva as a reflection of Brahman in the ego.

title: Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa
summary: Prakāśātman's sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikā, founding text of the Vivaraṇa school: Brahman is the locus and object of a positive (bhāva-rūpa) indescribable ignorance, established by perception, inference and presumption; the jīva is the reflection of Brahman, real and identical with its prototype; hearing is the principal means, enjoined by a restrictive injunction; the mahāvākya yields immediate knowledge.

title: Pañcapadyāni
summary: Five verses on the kinds of listeners to the Lord's stories.

title: Pañcappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā

attribution.tradition: rendered into Pali from the Sinhala commentaries (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, Mahāpaccarī, Kurundī and others) of the Mahāvihāra
attribution.scholarly: the extant Pali commentaries date from the 5th–6th c. and preserve older Sinhala material

summary: Buddhaghosa's commentary on the last five Abhidhamma books (Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, Paṭṭhāna); its Kathāvatthu section names the schools holding each refuted view.

title: Pañcaprakriyā
summary: A short work by Sarvajñātman on five topics of Advaita method.

title: Pañcārthabhāṣya
alt_titles: Kauṇḍinya's commentary on the Pāśupata Sūtra

attribution.tradition: 'Composed by the revered Kauṇḍinya' (colophon of each adhyāya).
attribution.scholarly: Kauṇḍinya, c. 4th–6th c. CE. Some scholars have identified him with the Pāśupata tīrthakara Rāśīkara, whose 'bhāṣya' the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha cites; the identification is uncertain.

structure.description: prose commentary on every sūtra, in five adhyāyas; opens with a verse naming Kauṇḍinya

summary: Kauṇḍinya's commentary reads the Pāśupata Sūtra as teaching five categories (effect, cause, union, rule, end of suffering), defines the Lord, the soul and the bonds, the three means of knowledge, the yamas and niyamas, the six 'doors' of feigned behaviour and the exchange of merit and sin, and correlates the sūtras with a five-stage path (residence, livelihood, strength, action, purification and gain for each stage). It holds that the end of suffering comes by the Lord's grace and that the Lord does not depend on karma.

title: Pāṇinīya Śikṣā
summary: The standard treatise of Vedic phonetics (śikṣā): it counts sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (v. 3), explains how speech arises when the self, having grasped meanings with the intellect, joins the mind to the wish to speak, the mind strikes the body's fire and the fire impels the breath (vv. 6–9), classifies sounds by place, effort, tone and duration, lists the faults and the virtues of reciters (vv. 32–33), pictures the six Vedāṅgas as the limbs of the Veda (vv. 41–42), warns that a mantra defective in accent or sound harms the sacrificer (v. 52), and ends in homage to Pāṇini, who received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara (v. 57).

attribution.tradition: Pāṇini

title: Paramapadasopānam

title: Paramārthasāra
summary: Abhinavagupta's 105 āryā verses retelling, 'by the view of Śiva's teaching' (v. 3), the older Ādhārakārikās / Paramārthasāra ascribed to Ādiśeṣa: the four eggs of manifestation, the Lord as the embodied enjoyer, the mirror image of the 36 tattvas, the kañcukas and the three coverings, bondage and liberation as Śiva's play, liberation as the manifestation of one's own power, the conduct and inner worship of the liberated, and the knower's death.

notes: Kiraṇa 10.14/10.19: Pārameśa to Śrīpūpa/Śrīrūpa → Uśanas. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Pārameśvara'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the necklace (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 26 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Śrīdevī (Kiraṇa: Śrīrūpa), then the sage Uśanas. The Kāmika assigns it 7 upabheda(s): Mataṅga, Yakṣiṇīpadma, Pārameśvara, Puṣkara, Suprayoga, Haṃsa, Sāmānya. Its best-known derivatives are the upāgamas Mataṅgapārameśvara and Pauṣkara. Reports of an early Nepalese 'Pārameśvara' manuscript were not verified in this pass.

notes: The number of views refuted (about twenty) and the exact list are given at moderate/low confidence.

title: Paramokṣanirāsakārikāvṛtti

title: Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra

title: Parātrīśikā
summary: A short Kaula-Trika dialogue: the Goddess asks how the Unsurpassed (anuttara) grants immediate Kaula perfection. Bhairava teaches the emanation of the letters as the tattvas (vv. 5-9), the Heart of Bhairava as the 'third Brahman' (10), the powers of reciting and remembering it (11-20), the tattvas from Kālāgni to Śiva (21-23), the universe resting in the Heart-seed as a banyan tree in its seed (24), initiation for one who knows this (25), and a worship procedure (26-33). It closes 'this is the Rudrayāmala' (35).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava; presents itself as belonging to the Rudrayāmala (final verse).

title: Paripāṭal

A precursor of Āḻvār devotion, not an Āḻvār text.
notes: Placed with lin:alvar as the earliest Tamil devotional hymns to Tirumāl; it belongs to Saṅgam literature, for which no lineage entry exists. Many poets; attributions per hymn are given in the colophons and not recorded here.

scholarly.text: later than the rest of the Vinaya, compiled in Sri Lanka (c. 1st c. BCE or later)

structure.description: about 19–21 sections (the count depends on the edition)

title: Parting from the Four Attachments (zhen pa bzhi bral)
summary: Four lines spoken by Mañjuśrī to the twelve-year-old Sachen Kunga Nyingpo in a vision: attachment to this life, to saṃsāra, to one's own purpose, and grasping, are each incompatible with dharma practice, renunciation, bodhicitta and the view — a summary of the whole path.

attribution.tradition: spoken by Mañjuśrī to Sachen at twelve, after six months of Mañjuśrī practice under Bari Lotsawa
attribution.scholarly: a Sakya instruction attested from Sachen's time and commented on by Drakpa Gyaltsen, Sakya Paṇḍita (?), Gorampa and many later masters

tradition.text: Sachen's twelfth year (c. 1104)

structure.description: four lines

editions.name: Tibetan: in the Sakya collected works and lojong compilations

title: Drakpa Gyaltsen's song on Parting from the Four Attachments (zhen pa bzhi bral gyi nyams len)
summary: Jetsün Drakpa Gyaltsen's song of experience expanding each of the four lines: the uselessness of ethics, study and meditation done for this life; the faults of the three realms; the futility of one's own liberation alone; and resting beyond the extremes of existence and non-existence.

title: Gorampa's guidance manual on Parting from the Four Attachments (zhen pa bzhi bral gyi khrid yig)
summary: A meditation manual arranging the four lines as a complete graded path from turning from this life to the view free of extremes.

title: Pāśupata Sūtra

attribution.tradition: Taught by the Lord (Bhagavat, Paśupati) who took a brahmin's body at Kāyāvataraṇa and taught Kuśika at Ujjayinī (Kauṇḍinya); later sources call the speaker Nakulīśa / Lakulīśa (Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha ch. 6).
attribution.scholarly: An anonymous sūtra text preserved only with Kauṇḍinya's commentary; composed before Kauṇḍinya. Its attribution to a historical Lakulīśa is the tradition's.

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva incarnate as Lakulīśa

scholarly.text: before Kauṇḍinya (4th–6th c.); often placed in the early centuries CE

structure.description: five adhyāyas of short sūtras - 44, 27, 26, 24 and 47 in the Sagar-based numbering (168 in all, with a lacuna at 5.29); 167 in the Sastri-based numbering. Each adhyāya closes with one of the five brahma-mantras (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna).

summary: The root text of the Pāśupatas. Adhyāya 1 prescribes the first-stage observance in the temple (ash-bathing thrice daily, lying in ash, wearing the used garland, the six-limbed offering of laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅkāra sound, prostration and muttering) and lists the powers that arise; adhyāyas 2-4 teach worship of Rudra alone, courting dishonour by feigned madness and the transfer of merit and sin, and non-return; adhyāya 5 teaches the solitary yogin in empty houses, caves and cremation grounds, meditation on Oṃ in the heart, constant remembrance of Rudra and the end of suffering by the Lord's grace.

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Vaiśravaṇa asks Brahmā (Svayambhū): the inner sacrifice of the haṃsa, the praṇava as thread, Paśupati as the witness who empowers the senses, and non-dual knowledge; non-injury as the true sacrifice; purity of food purifies mind.

title: Patiṉoṉṟām Tirumuṟai (the eleventh book)
summary: Forty works by twelve poets: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār's three poems, Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ's three, Aiyaṭikaḷ Kāṭavarkōṉ's Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā, Nakkīrar's Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai and other poems, Kallāṭar, Kapilar, Paraṇar, Iḷampperumāṉ Aṭikaḷ, Atiravāciyaṭikaḷ, Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār's five poems, and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi's ten works including the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti.

structure.description: 40 works by 12 authors (moderate confidence)

notes: Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of this book is often distinguished by scholars from the later Siddhar Paṭṭiṉattār (tch:pattinattar, U22); the tradition often identifies them.

title: Paṭisambhidāmagga
summary: The 'path of discrimination', an Abhidhamma-style treatise in the Sutta Piṭaka ascribed to Sāriputta: 73 kinds of knowledge, ānāpānasati, the faculties, emptiness, the kinds of liberation and the 'path of discrimination'.

structure.description: 3 vaggas (Mahā, Yuganaddha, Paññā), 30 kathās

tradition.text: spoken by Sāriputta

notes: Treated in depth by U37 with the Visuddhimagga, which draws on it.

title: Patna Dharmapada

structure.description: 22 chapters, c. 414 verses

summary: A Dharmapada in a Prakrit-like language from a manuscript photographed in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana; its school has been proposed to be the Saṃmitīya (scholarly hypothesis).

editions.name: M. Cone (JPTS 1989), GRETIL e-text

title: Patnī-prasāda
summary: Aṅkīyā nāṭ on the Brahmin wives who fed Kṛṣṇa against their husbands' ritual scruples: devotion over ritual. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

title: Patrāvalambana
summary: A short polemical text Vallabha is said to have posted at the Viśvanātha temple in Kāśī, challenging rival Vedāntins on the unity of the Vedic karma and jñāna sections under Brahmavāda.

title: Paṭṭhāna

attribution.tradition: The tradition's account (Atthasālinī, Nidānakathā): the Buddha taught the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven during the rains retreat after the Twin Miracle, to the gods led by his mother; each day he gave the method (naya) to Sāriputta at Lake Anotatta, who taught it to his five hundred pupils; it was recited at the First Council. When the Buddha contemplated the Paṭṭhāna in the fourth week after awakening, rays of six colours issued from his body (Atthasālinī).
attribution.scholarly: the latest and largest Abhidhamma book

structure.description: Paccayuddesa and Paccayaniddesa of 24 conditions; applied in the Tika-, Duka-, Dukatika-, Tikaduka-, Tikatika- and Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna, each in anuloma, paccanīya, anuloma-paccanīya and paccanīya-anuloma modes (24 'paṭṭhānas')

summary: 'Conditional Relations' (the Mahāpakaraṇa): sets out twenty-four modes of conditionality (paccaya) and applies them, positively and negatively, to all the triads and dyads of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix — the Abhidhamma's full account of how dhammas condition one another.

title: Paṭṭiṉattār pāṭalkaḷ (Tiruppāṭal tiraṭṭu)
summary: The songs ascribed to the renouncer Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar): the Tiruvēkampamālai to Śiva at Kāñcī, the Tillai verses, three Kōyil tiruvakavals, the Kacci tiruvakaval and the Aruṭpulampal, with further 'general' songs and the songs at his mother's cremation. Themes: impermanence, the body as a pot of filth, renunciation, women as snare, karma, and refuge in Śiva's feet.

tradition.text: the tradition makes the renouncer a merchant of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam in the Cōḻa age

scholarly.text: the Siddhar songs are usually placed c. 14th–17th c. and distinguished from Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai (c. 10th c.)

structure.description: 8 sections in the local edition: Tiruvēkampamālai (42 + 1 viruttam), Tiruttillai, three Kōyil tiruvakavals, Kacci tiruvakaval, two Aruṭpulampals

notes: Section list checked in the local e-text. The mother's-cremation songs and the 'eyeless needle' verse are recalled from other editions (not in the local file).

title: Pauliśa Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta of Puliśa, known from the Pañcasiddhāntikā and cited by later authors; Varāhamihira calls it accurate.
notes: Known chiefly through Varāhamihira's Pañcasiddhāntikā.

title: Paumacariu of Svayambhū
summary: Svayambhūdeva's Apabhraṃśa Rāmāyaṇa (9th c.), following Raviṣeṇa; Svayambhū also wrote the Riṭṭhaṇemicariu on Neminātha and Kṛṣṇa. Some scholars connect him with the Yāpanīyas (low confidence).

title: Paumacariya
summary: Vimalasūri's Prakrit Jain Rāmāyaṇa: Rāma (Padma) is a non-violent Jain hero who ends as a liberated monk; Lakṣmaṇa, the vāsudeva, kills Rāvaṇa, a learned vidyādhara rather than a demon; the text rejects the 'false' features of other Rāma stories.

tradition.text: 530 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa, according to its own colophon

title: Pauṣkarāgama
notes: Do not confuse with src:pauskara-samhita (Pāñcarātra).
summary: A Śaiva upāgama of the Pārameśvara (the Kāmika's 'Puṣkara'), whose jñānapāda was commented on by Umāpati Śivācārya and Jñānaprakāśa; distinct from the Pāñcarātra Pauṣkara Saṃhitā.

title: Pauṣkara Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: revealed by Bhagavān (Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva); one of the traditional 108 saṃhitās

structure.description: 43 adhyāyas (as usually reported)

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00259; GRETIL adhyāyas 27–43

notes: Distinct from the Śaiva src:pauskara-agama.
summary: One of the three gems of the Pāñcarātra, in which Bhagavān instructs Pauṣkara (the lotus-born Brahmā); rich in maṇḍala and ritual material. The Pārameśvara Saṃhitā is its expansion, followed at Śrīraṅgam.

title: Pauṣkarabhāṣya
summary: Umāpati Śivācārya's commentary on the jñānapāda of the Śaiva Pauṣkarāgama.

title: Pauṣkaravṛtti
summary: Jñānaprakāśa's commentary on the Pauṣkara's jñānapāda (manuscript with the Daśakārya and Prāsādaṣaṭślokī).

title: Soma Pavamāna hymns (Ṛgveda book 9)
summary: The ninth maṇḍala: 114 hymns to Soma 'self-purifying' (pavamāna) as the juice flows through the woollen filter, gathered from all the priestly families. The book ends with Kaśyapa's prayer to be made immortal in the world of inexhaustible light (9.113); its own verses say that whoever studies these pāvamānī verses eats purified food (9.67.31).

checks.note: Local count: maṇḍala 9 has 114 hymns; 9.113 (Kaśyapa Mārīca) and 9.67.31 (header '31–32 pavamānyadhyetā') confirmed.

title: Periya Purāṇam
summary: Cēkkiḻār's 'Great Purāṇa' (Tiruttoṇṭar Purāṇam): the lives of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and the nine groups of devotees named in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai, framed by Cuntarar's own story; the twelfth Tirumuṟai and the charter of Tamil Śaiva sainthood.

title: Puṣṭipravāhamaryādābheda
summary: On the differences between the three kinds of souls and paths: grace (puṣṭi), rule (maryādā) and worldly stream (pravāha).

title: Puttamaṃsa Sutta
summary: The four nutriments with their similes: edible food like a son's flesh eaten in the desert, contact like a flayed cow, volition like a charcoal pit, consciousness like a criminal struck by three hundred spears.

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

editions.name: Bhikkhu Sujato (English), SuttaCentral

notes: SuttaCentral uid sn12.63; Mahāsaṅgīti title 'Puttamaṁsasutta' (checked locally).

title: Qissa Pūran Bhagat
summary: Punjabi verse romance of Pūraṇ Bhagat, son of Rājā Salvāhan of Sialkot, maimed at his stepmother Lūṇā's false accusation, restored by Gorakhnāth and made a yogī — identified in Nāth tradition with Cauraṅgīnāth.
notes: Best-known version by Qādaryār (19th c., recalled). Context for the Cauraṅgī legend.

title: Rādhā-sudhānidhi (Rādhā-rasa-sudhānidhi)
summary: About 270 Sanskrit verses of praise and longing addressed to Rādhā as the supreme goddess of love, whose favour even Kṛṣṇa seeks; recited in both the Rādhāvallabha and Gauḍīya traditions.

attribution.tradition: The Rādhāvallabhīs ascribe it to Hita Harivaṃśa; the Gauḍīyas to Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī.
attribution.scholarly: Authorship unresolved.

structure.description: about 270 verses

title: Rāgavartmacandrikā
summary: Viśvanātha's short treatise on spontaneous devotion (rāgānugā): eager longing (lobha) as its sole qualification and the method of serving in one's practitioner's body and inner perfected body.

title: Rāgamayīkaṇā

attribution.tradition: anonymous or not recalled
attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text on rāga (passionate love) as the way (low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Rāgavibodha of Somanātha
summary: Somanātha's treatise on the classification and ornamentation of rāgas on the vīṇā.

title: Rahasyarakṣā
summary: Deśika's commentary on Yāmuna's Stotraratna and Catuḥślokī and on Rāmānuja's Gadyas, defending Śrī's supremacy and the doctrine of surrender.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Rahasyatrayasāra
summary: Deśika's Maṇipravāḷa summa of the Śrīvaiṣṇava way of surrender, in 32 chapters (adhikāras): the five things to be known, the three realities, the supreme deity, the qualified, prapatti with its limbs as an independent means, conduct after surrender, offences and their removal, departure and the path of light, the three secret mantras, and the duties of teacher and disciple.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Raidās Paracaī

attribution.tradition: by Anantadās
attribution.scholarly: late 16th c.

summary: Anantadās's life of Raidās: the leatherworker devotee of Banaras, his humility and poverty, the brahmins' hostility, the proof of his sanctity and the queen of Chittor (Jhālī) who becomes his disciple.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert & P. G. Friedlander, The Life and Works of Raidās (1992)

title: Raihai tokuzui (Paying Homage and Obtaining the Marrow)
summary: One should bow to whoever has attained the Way, whether man or woman, old or young; criticises exclusion of women from sacred places and from teaching.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Rāja Nighaṇṭu
summary: Narahari Paṇḍita's large lexicon of medicinal substances.

title: Rājadharma (Rājadharmānuśāsanaparvan)

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: composed and expanded in stages, c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

structure.description: 128 chapters (CE 12.1–128), about 4,500 verse units

summary: Bhīṣma's instruction to Yudhiṣṭhira on the dharma of kings: the origin of kingship and of the science of punishment (daṇḍanīti), protection of subjects, counsel, taxation, war, and the duties of the varṇas and āśramas; preceded by the family's arguments persuading Yudhiṣṭhira not to renounce.

title: Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti)

scholarly.text: first half of the 11th c. CE (reign of Bhoja of Dhārā, c. 1010–1055)

summary: King Bhoja's concise vṛtti on the sūtras (not on the bhāṣya). It sets out the four samprajñāta samādhis as savitarka, savicāra, sānanda and sāsmita, calls those who rest content in bliss 'videhas' and those who rest in I-am-ness 'prakṛtilayas', and treats discernment of the supreme puruṣa as the grasper-coalescence (1.17); asamprajñāta is reached by rejecting every arising activity 'not this, not this' (1.18); devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher without desire for fruit (1.23, 2.1).

title: Rājapraśnīya
summary: The second Upāṅga: the god Sūryābha's visit to Mahāvīra and his worship of Jina images in his celestial palace, and the dialogue in which Keśin, of Pārśva's line, convinces King Paesi (Pradeśin), who had tried to find the soul by experiments on criminals, that the soul is distinct from the body.
notes: The Paesi dialogue parallels the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23) of the Pali canon, where the Buddhist monk Kumāra Kassapa answers King Pāyāsi.
alt_summary: An upāṅga of the Jain canon. Its second part is the dialogue of the monk Kesi Kumāra (of Pārśva's line) with King Paesi (Pradeśin) of Seyaviyā, who holds that soul and body are the same and supports it with experiments on criminals; Kesi answers with similes, the king converts, is poisoned by his queen, and becomes the god Sūriyābha.
alt_notes: Not available locally; from memory. Closely parallel to the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23).

title: Rājaśēkharavilāsa (Ṣaḍakṣaradēva)
summary: A seventeenth-century Kannada campū narrating a Śaiva devotional legend, a classic of later Vīraśaiva poetry.

title: Rājavārttika (Sāṃkhya)

attribution.tradition: unknown
attribution.scholarly: Lost work quoted by Vācaspati Miśra (Tattvakaumudī on SK 72) for the verses enumerating the sixty topics; author unknown.

summary: A lost Sāṃkhya work known from Vācaspati Miśra's quotation of its verses listing the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra (ten fundamental topics and the fifty).
notes: Quotation recalled from the Tattvakaumudī on SK 72 (not in the local partial text).

title: Rajjab kī Vāṇī

attribution.tradition: Rajjab's own sākhīs and padas

summary: Rajjab's own verse on the guru, the Name and renunciation, by the Pathan disciple who left his wedding procession to follow Dādū.

title: Raktayamāri Tantra
summary: Tantra of Red Yamāri; transmitted in the Virūpa lineage to the Sakya.

editions.name: Derge Kangyur, Tōh 474 (confirmed in the local Derge catalogue)

title: Rāma Gītā

attribution.tradition: Rāma's teaching to Lakṣmaṇa, 'churned from the ocean of the Upaniṣads' (AR Māhātmya), narrated by Śiva to Pārvatī
attribution.scholarly: part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; a compact Advaita manual

scholarly.text: with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, c. 14th-15th c. CE

structure.description: one sarga of 62 verses

summary: After one's duties have purified the mind, one should approach a true guru: ignorance is the root of rebirth and only knowledge removes it, not action, so knowledge cannot be combined with ritual action; the meaning of 'that thou art' is grasped by partial implication; the self is distinct from the three bodies and three states; superimposition is explained; one meditates on the Self, dissolves the syllables of Oṃ into it, lives out prārabdha free of ego and merges in Rāma. Until all is seen as Rāma, one should worship him.

editions.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Gita Press); Gītāsaṅgraha (Poona 1915)

attribution.tradition: Rāma's teaching to Hanumān
attribution.scholarly: late; distinct from the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa's Rāma Gītā

summary: A longer Rāma Gītā (recalled as 18 chapters) in which Rāma teaches Hanumān Vedānta and yoga; distinct from the 62-verse Rāma Gītā of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
notes: Recalled only; flagged for the hallucination sweep.

title: Rāma-hṛdaya
location_in_parent: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Bālakāṇḍa 1 (Sītā's teaching 1.1.31-43; Rāma's 1.1.44-52; named at 1.1.53)

attribution.tradition: Rāma's own teaching to Hanumān after the coronation, introduced by Sītā; Śiva calls it the essence of all Vedānta
attribution.scholarly: part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa

scholarly.text: with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, c. 14th-15th c. CE

summary: Sītā tells Hanumān that Rāma is the non-dual Brahman and she the primal nature who does all the deeds attributed to him; Rāma then teaches the threefold consciousness (the whole, the consciousness delimited by the intellect, and its reflection) by the example of the threefold sky, and that the great sayings reveal the identity whose knowledge destroys ignorance, provided one has devotion.

checks.note: Colophon 'bālakāṇḍe śrīrāmahṛdayaṃ nāma prathamaḥ sargaḥ' and 1.1.53 'etat te 'bhihitaṃ devi śrīrāmahṛdayaṃ' verified; Sītā speaks 1.1.32-43 and Rāma 1.1.44-52.

title: Rāma-vijaya

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Vālmīki after Nārada told him Rāma's story; the first śloka arose from his grief at a hunter's killing of one of a pair of krauñca birds (1.2.15–18); sung by Rāma's sons Kuśa and Lava.
attribution.scholarly: An oral-bardic work fixed in writing over centuries; the first and seventh books are widely held to be later additions; transmitted in northern and southern recensions.

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki in the Tretā yuga, in Rāma's own time

structure.description: 7 books (kāṇḍas). The poem itself speaks of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, six books and the Uttara (1.4.2, vulgate). The local southern vulgate text has Bāla 77, Ayodhyā 119, Araṇya 75, Kiṣkindhā 67, Sundara 68, Yuddha 128, Uttara 111 sargas. The Baroda critical edition (1960–75) constitutes a shorter text.

summary: The first poem (ādikāvya): the life of Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā — his exile in obedience to his father's word, the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, the alliance with the monkeys and Hanumān, the war in Laṅkā, his righteous reign, and (in the last book) the banishment of Sītā. It presents Rāma as dharma embodied: truth to one's word, obedience to parents, fraternal loyalty, protection of those who seek refuge, and the king's duty to his subjects.

title: Rāmcaritmānas
summary: Tulsīdās's Awadhi retelling of the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas (Bāla, Ayodhyā, Araṇya, Kiṣkindhā, Sundara, Laṅkā, Uttara), framed by four nested dialogues (Śiva–Pārvatī, Kākabhuśuṇḍi–Garuḍa, Yājñavalkya–Bharadvāja, the poet and his hearers) likened to the four ghāṭs of a lake. It teaches that Rāma is the supreme Brahman, formless and with form; that his name is greater than either form; that devotion (bhakti) with the saints' company is the easiest and surest path in the Kali age; and it depicts dharma embodied in Rāma and Rāma-rājya.

title: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: hymns (sūktas) of praise and invocation to Agni, Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, the Aśvins, Uṣas, Rudra, Viṣṇu and others, recited by the hotṛ priest. Beside the liturgy it contains speculative hymns on the One (1.164, 10.129, 10.121, 10.90, 10.125), on speech, on the self and on death and the fathers (10.14–18).

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; each hymn's seer (ṛṣi), deity and metre are recorded by the Anukramaṇīs
attribution.scholarly: composed by priestly poet families over several centuries and redacted into the Śākala recension

tradition.text: beginningless; the hymns were 'seen' by the ṛṣis and handed down (Nirukta 1.20)

scholarly.text: c. 1500–1000 BCE; family books (2–7) earliest, books 1 and 10 latest

structure.description: 10 maṇḍalas; 1,028 sūktas counting the 11 Vālakhilya hymns (8.49–59); c. 10,550 verses (counts differ slightly). Books 2–7 are the family books: 2 Gṛtsamada, 3 Viśvāmitra, 4 Vāmadeva, 5 Atri, 6 Bharadvāja, 7 Vasiṣṭha; book 8 chiefly the Kāṇvas (and Āṅgirasas); book 9 the hymns to Soma Pavamāna gathered from all families; books 1 and 10 are collections of many seers and are regarded as later. A second division into 8 aṣṭakas × 8 adhyāyas (64 adhyāyas) and vargas is used for recitation.

title: Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)

Most traditional and modern readings of the Ṛgveda start from it.

summary: Haribhadra's 87-verse compendium presenting six darśanas — Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā) — each by its deity, categories and means of knowledge, without polemic, adding the Lokāyata at the end for those who count Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika as one. Commented by Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā).
notes: Id already used by U11/U17; U35 adds the Jain view of the other darśanas.
alt_summary: Haribhadra's short verse survey of the six systems (Buddhist, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Jain, Vaiśeṣika, Jaiminīya) with the Lokāyata added at the end (since some count Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika as one). The Lokāyata verses state that there is no soul, no release, no merit or demerit; that the world extends only as far as the senses reach ('see the wolf's footprint, my dear'); that one should eat and drink since what is past does not return; and that consciousness arises from the four elements like intoxication from the ingredients of liquor.

title: Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra
summary: The Lotus Sūtra: the Buddha reveals that the three vehicles were skillful means and there is only the one buddha-vehicle; all who hear it, even with a single flower or a child's drawing of a stūpa, will become buddhas; the śrāvakas receive predictions of buddhahood. Through the parables of the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, the conjured city, the jewel in the robe and the physician's sons it teaches skillful means; the stūpa of the past buddha Prabhūtaratna appears; the nāga princess becomes a buddha instantly; bodhisattvas rise from the earth; the Buddha reveals that he awakened incalculable aeons ago and his lifespan is immeasurable; it praises the dharma-preacher, Sadāparibhūta, Bhaiṣajyarāja's self-offering, Avalokiteśvara's rescue and Samantabhadra's protection.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

title: Sāmaveda Saṃhitā (Kauthuma)
summary: The Veda of chants: verses (ṛc), nearly all taken from the Ṛgveda (mostly books 8 and 9), arranged as the texts (yoni) of melodies (sāman) sung by the udgātṛ priests at the soma sacrifice. The verse-books (ārcika) are the libretto; the melodies themselves are in the song-books (gāna). The tradition treats the Sāmaveda as the root of chant and of music.

attribution.tradition: authorless (apauruṣeya) revelation seen by the ṛṣis; arranged by Vyāsa; Jaimini received the Sāmaveda from Vyāsa (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21)
attribution.scholarly: a liturgical anthology drawn largely from the Ṛgveda, arranged for the udgātṛ's chants

structure.description: Pūrvārcika (āgneya, aindra and pāvamāna parvans; then the Āraṇyaka section and the Mahānāmnī verses; c. 650 verses) and Uttarārcika (c. 1,225 verses in groups, mostly triplets); about 1,875 verses in the usual Kauthuma count (c. 1,800 in Griffith's edition), only some 75 not found in the Ṛgveda (counts differ).

title: Samayasāra
summary: Kundakunda's treatise on the pure self (samaya): from the standpoint of ultimate reality (niścaya) the soul is a pure knower, untouched by karma, neither doer nor enjoyer of material karma, while the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra), which ascribes bondage, conduct and stages to it, is needed only to teach. It proceeds through the nine categories (soul and non-soul, doer and deed, merit and demerit, inflow, stopping, shedding, bondage, liberation) to the all-pure knowledge.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Kundakunda (Padmanandin), who according to Digambara legend visited the living Tīrthaṅkara Sīmandhara in Videha; the Digambara tradition places him in the 1st c. BCE / 1st c. CE and ranks him immediately after Mahāvīra and Gautama in the auspicious verse ('maṅgalaṃ bhagavān vīro maṅgalaṃ gautamo gaṇī / maṅgalaṃ kundakundāryo jainadharmo 'stu maṅgalam').
attribution.scholarly: Scholarly dates for Kundakunda range from the 2nd to the 8th c. CE; the corpus ascribed to him may not be from a single hand.

summary: The classical root text of Sāṃkhya. summary: The sūtra text of later Sāṃkhya. scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

Paṭala 1 gives the cosmogony of sound — Śakti, nāda and bindu from the supreme Lord (1.7), the threefold bindu (1.8–9), śabda-brahman as the consciousness of all beings (1.11–13), dwelling as kuṇḍalinī and manifesting as the letters (1.14) — and the fifty letters with their deities; paṭala 2 gives the classes of mantras, their fifty defects (2.64–70), the ten purifications (2.112–122), and the marks of guru and disciple and the period of testing (2.141–153); later paṭalas give the mantras, worship and puraścaraṇa of many deities, and the last paṭala treats yoga.

structure.description: sixteen chapters presenting sixteen systems in ascending order, ending with Śaṅkara's Advaita; ch. 6 on the Nakulīśa-Pāśupatas

summary: Its sixth chapter presents the Pāśupata system in its own terms: the five categories with their subdivisions, the twofold end of suffering (cessation, and the Lord's powers of knowing and acting), the vows and six 'doors', the Gaṇakārikā's pentads (quoted as Haradatta's), the Pāśupata claims of distinctiveness, and a defence of the Lord's independence from karma.

editions.name: ch. 6 reprinted as appendix II to Dalal, GOS 15 (1920); Muktabodha M00508

alt_summary: Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): its ninth chapter, the Raseśvaradarśana, presents the rasa doctrine as a Māheśvara system — jīvanmukti through a body made stable by mercury, mercury and mica as the seeds of Śiva and Gaurī, the eighteen processings of mercury (named but not explained), dehavedha rather than gold as the aim, and yoga in the stable body leading to the vision of the light between the brows — quoting the Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdaya and the Raseśvarasiddhānta.

A 14th-century Advaita doxography of sixteen systems; its fifth chapter, 'Pūrṇaprajña-darśana', is an early outside summary of Madhva's system (the five differences, Viṣṇu's supremacy, the gradation of souls).

A doxography of sixteen systems, from the Cārvāka through the Buddhist, Jain, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, grammatical, Sāṃkhya and Yoga schools, each refuted by the next, ending with (a reference to) Advaita as the culmination.

U33 contribution: its first chapter, the Cārvāka-darśana, is the fullest classical summary of the Lokāyata — the four elements, consciousness from the elements like intoxicating power, the self as the body qualified by consciousness, pleasure as the only aim, perception as the only means of knowledge (with a long critique of invariable concomitance), svabhāva as the cause of variety, and a closing series of verses ascribed to Bṛhaspati against sacrifice, funeral offerings and the Veda.

U31 contribution: its chapter on the Pāṇini-darśana presents grammar as a school of liberation — the sphoṭa as the eternal meaning-bearer, the word-brahman, and grammar as the door to release, quoting the Vākyapadīya.
notes: U30 contribution only: the Raseśvara chapter (ch. 9). Authorship and dating as given by the owning units.
alt_notes: Chapter order (Pūrṇaprajña 5th) recalled at moderate confidence.

title: Sarvasiddhāntasaṅgraha (Sarvadarśanasiddhāntasaṅgraha)
summary: A verse doxography ascribed to Śaṅkara that sets out the doctrines of the schools from the Lokāyata upward. Its Lokāyata section states in verse that the four elements are the only principles, that consciousness arises from them like intoxicating power, that pleasure from embraces is the human aim and pain from thorns is hell, that the lord is the king known to the world and liberation is the destruction of the body.

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram, Rudrādhyāya)
summary: The litany of homage to Rudra in his hundreds of forms: after asking Rudra to turn his wrath, bow and arrows away and to show his auspicious, non-terrible body (śivā tanūḥ aghorā), it pays homage (namaḥ) to Rudra as lord of paths, forests, hosts and animals, as present in thieves and craftsmen, in the small and the great, in waters, clouds and grass, and ends by placing the countless Rudras on earth far away. Its eighth section contains 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca', the source the Śaiva traditions give for the five-syllable formula.
notes: Used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra; recited in the tradition as Rudra-japa (Ekādaśa-, Laghu-, Mahā-, Atirudra) and in Śaiva worship. The Jābāla Upaniṣad names śatarudrīya recitation as a means to immortality (reference only).

The Jābāla Upaniṣad reference and the Rudra-japa multiples are side notes (multiples confirmed under prc:rudra-japa).

title: Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama
summary: The oldest Digambara scripture, in six parts (Jīvasthāna, Kṣudrakabandha, Bandhasvāmitvavicaya, Vedanā, Vargaṇā, Mahābandha), analysing souls through the fourteen stages of quality (guṇasthāna) and fourteen 'ways of search' (mārgaṇā), and the bondage of karma in minute detail. It opens with the Namaskāra mantra. Tradition says it preserves part of the Agrāyaṇīya Pūrva (the Karmaprābhṛta) taught by Dharasena.

attribution.tradition: Dharasena, who knew part of the Pūrvas, taught the Karmaprābhṛta at the Candra cave on Girinagar (Girnār) to Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali; Puṣpadanta composed the opening (the Satprarūpaṇā) and Bhūtabali the rest, 683 years after the nirvāṇa; completion is celebrated on Śruta Pañcamī.
attribution.scholarly: c. 2nd–5th c. CE (low confidence)

summary: One of the 'three gems' (ratnatraya) of the Pāñcarātra, regarded as among the oldest saṃhitās. The Īśvara Saṃhitā is its ritual expansion (Melkote).

summary: Bhāskararāya's commentary on the Lalitā Sahasranāma. title: Saundaryalaharī
summary: A hymn of one hundred verses to the Goddess. The first part (verses 1-41, called the Ānandalaharī) teaches the doctrine: Śiva can act only when joined to Śakti, the Goddess's ascent through the six cakras and return as kuṇḍalinī, the structure of the Śrīcakra, the coded Śrīvidyā mantra, the Goddess as Śiva's body, and her presence in each cakra; the second part describes her beauty from crown to foot and ends by offering the hymn made of her own words back to her.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. In the common legend Śaṅkara received a hymn of a hundred verses at Kailāsa; Nandin (in other versions Gaṇeśa) snatched it, leaving the first forty-one, and Śaṅkara composed the rest.
attribution.scholarly: Authorship by the Advaita teacher of the Brahma Sūtra commentary is doubted; the text is well established by the time of its 16th-c. commentators.

structure.description: 100 verses in śikhariṇī metre (some editions 103); 1-41 doctrinal (Ānandalaharī), 42-100 descriptive (from crown to foot)

summary: Dōgen's Japanese-language essays (1231–1253) on the buddha-way: zazen as the realization of buddhahood, the realized kōan, being-time, buddha-nature, dharma transmission, the monastic life, cause and effect, and the teachings of the ancestors.
notes: Not held locally (T82 no. 2582). Fascicles are entered as separate sources with part_of src:shobogenzo.

summary: Ejō's notes (1235–1238) of Dōgen's informal talks: give up body and life for the Dharma, practise just sitting, abandon fame and gain.

title: Shōji (Birth and Death)
summary: Because there is buddha in birth-and-death there is no birth-and-death; birth-and-death is the life of the buddha; neither cling nor reject; throw body and mind into the house of the buddha.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Hymn of True Entrusting and the Nenbutsu (Shōshin nenbutsu ge)
summary: The hymn recited daily in Shinshū: homage to Amida; the vow and the name as the rightly determined act and shinjin as the cause; the evil and good ordinary beings who hear and entrust being called white lotuses; then the teachings of the seven masters from Nāgārjuna to Hōnen.

title: Hymns of the Dharma Ages (Shōzōmatsu wasan)
summary: Hymns composed in old age on the three ages of the Dharma, doubt of the Buddha's wisdom, and Shinran's lament over his own untruthful heart; with the appended note on jinen hōni in some versions.
notes: The three are together called the Sanjō wasan.

title: Shukke kudoku (The Merit of Leaving Home)

title: Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi

It sets out Vīraśaiva doctrine as Śivādvaita consistent with Veda and Āgama and maps the path as 101 sthalas (44 on the side of the soul, 57 on the side of the liṅga) under the six great sthalas from bhakta to aikya.

structure.description: 21 chapters (pariccheda); ch. 1 frame and author's lineage; 2–4 descent of Reṇuka and meeting with Agastya; 5–14 the 44 aṅga-sthalas under bhakta (15), māheśvara (9), prasādi (7), prāṇaliṅgi (5), śaraṇa (4), aikya (4); 15–20 the 57 liṅga-sthalas; 21 Reṇuka's dialogue with Vibhīṣaṇa and his return into the liṅga

title: Śrībhāṣya
summary: Rāmānuja's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras following, he says, Bodhāyana's lost Vṛtti. Its first sūtra contains the 'great prior view' (mahāpūrvapakṣa) of Advaita and its refutation (mahāsiddhānta), including the seven untenables of avidyā; the whole establishes Brahman as the qualified cause of the world, the soul as its mode, bhakti-meditation as the means and liberation as reaching Brahman by the path of light.

tradition.text: Rāmānuja, 1017–1137 CE (traditional)

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas × 4 pādas, following the sūtras (Rāmānuja's sūtra division differs slightly from Śaṅkara's)

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Śrīkaṇṭha (Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya)

tradition.text: Vīraśaiva tradition: very early (before Śaṅkara)

title: Śrīkarabhāṣya
summary: Śrīpati Paṇḍita's Vīraśaiva commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, naming the doctrine Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita: the non-duality of Śiva (liṅga) and the soul (aṅga), both qualified by Śakti, realised as their union (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya).

title: Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanāda-sūtra

title: Sūrya Siddhānta
summary: The most authoritative siddhānta: a dialogue in which a being born of the Sun's portion teaches the asura Maya the motions of the planets. It gives the units of time, the yugas and the kalpa, mean and true planetary positions, eclipses, conjunctions, heliacal risings, the cosmography of the earth-globe held in space by Brahman's power, instruments, and the nine measures of time.

attribution.tradition: revealed by the Sun, through a person born of his portion, to Maya at the end of the Kṛta age (SS 1.2–9)
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; an early version was summarized by Varāhamihira (Pañcasiddhāntikā); the extant text was revised c. 800–1000 CE

tradition.text: taught at the close of the Kṛta yuga (SS 1.2)

scholarly.text: extant recension c. 8th–11th c. CE; an earlier Saura-siddhānta by the 6th c.

structure.description: 14 chapters (adhikāra), c. 500 verses: mean motions; true places; direction, place and time; lunar eclipse; solar eclipse; projection of eclipses; planetary conjunctions; conjunctions with asterisms; heliacal risings and settings; the moon's horns; the pātas; cosmography (bhūgola); instruments (jyotiṣopaniṣad); measures of time

notes: Commentaries: Raṅganātha's Gūḍhārthaprakāśa (1603), Parameśvara, Kamalākara. Local e-text: GRETIL suryasiddhanta.

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
summary: The second Aṅga, largely polemical: it states and rejects the views of other teachers (materialists, the one-self doctrine, the soul-is-the-body doctrine, non-agency, fatalism, Buddhist momentariness), classifies all rival doctrines under four heads (kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñānavāda, vinayavāda), warns the monk against temptations, praises Mahāvīra, and in Book II gives the parable of the lotus, Ārdraka's debates with rival ascetics and the Nālandā dialogue with a follower of Pārśva.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

scholarly.text: Book I old (verse; often placed c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE), Book II later

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 16 lectures (mostly verse), II = 7 lectures (mostly prose)

alt_summary: U33 contribution: the second aṅga is the Jain canon's main report of rival doctrines. Book 1 ch. 1 reviews the five-element view, the one-self view, the view that soul and body are the same, the non-agent self, the five elements with the self as sixth, the Buddhist momentary aggregates, fixed destiny (saṅgatiya), ignorance (annāṇa), the kiriyāvāda of intention, and the creation views; ch. 12 names the four 'assemblies' of disputants (kiriya, akiriya, viṇaya, annāṇa). Book 2 ch. 1 (the lotus) and ch. 6 (Ārdraka's debates with Gosāla, the Buddhists, brāhmaṇas and elephant-ascetics) continue the review.

alt_summary: Śīlāṅka's Sanskrit commentary on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, which identifies and explains the rival doctrines the text refutes.

Mūrtipūjakas count forty-five texts (11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 10 Prakīrṇakas, 6 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras, 2 Cūlikāsūtras); Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs accept thirty-two. The Digambaras hold that the original Aṅgas were lost and do not accept this collection.

attribution.tradition: The Aṅgas go back to the gaṇadharas' composition of Mahāvīra's teaching; the aṅgabāhya texts to later elders (sthaviras); recited at the councils of Pāṭaliputra, Mathurā and Valabhī and written down at Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa).
attribution.scholarly: Compiled from materials of very different ages (c. 4th c. BCE – 5th c. CE); the grouping into Upāṅgas, Chedas, Mūlas and Prakīrṇakas and the count of 45 are medieval (the Nandī classifies differently: aṅga-praviṣṭa / aṅga-bāhya, kālika / utkālika).

title: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta's encyclopaedic exposition of the Trika on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, integrating Kaula and Krama. After defining bondage as ignorance and knowledge as the sole cause of liberation (1.22-23), it orders all Śaiva practice by the four means (chs. 2-5), sets out time, space, the tattvas and the paths of manifestation (6-12), the descent of grace (13), the whole ritual of initiation, consecration, funerary and daily rites (14-28), the secret Kula ritual (29), mantra, maṇḍala and mudrā (30-32), and ends with unification, the harmony of the scriptures, the lineage and the author's account of himself (33-37).

structure.description: 37 āhnikas (chapters), c. 5,800 verses; chapter topics per Abhinavagupta's own table of contents (TĀ 1.278-329) and colophons: 1 vijñānabheda (the kinds of knowledge; knowledge as the cause of liberation; table of contents); 2 anupāya (the means-less); 3 śāmbhavopāya (the reflection of the universe in consciousness; the letters); 4 śāktopāya (purification of thought, sattarka, the wheel of consciousness, the twelve Kālīs, critique of rules); 5 āṇavopāya (meditation, uccāra of prāṇa, the seven ānandas, the five signs, karaṇa, varṇa); 6 kālopāya / kālatattva (time in the breath and its cycles); 7 cakrodaya (the arising of the wheels; mantra and breath counts); 8 deśādhvan (the path of space: the worlds); 9 tattvādhvan (the path of the tattvas); 10 tattvabheda (divisions of the tattvas; the states and the seven pramātṛs); 11 kalādhvan (the path of the kalās; letters and mantras); 12 adhvopayoga (use of the paths); 13 śaktipāta (the descent of power; its grades); 14 dīkṣopakrama (preliminaries of initiation; removal of concealment); 15 samayadīkṣā (initiation into the samaya; the samaya rules); 16 prameya (the putraka initiation and the knowables purified); 17 vikṣipta/extended initiation (cord, purification of the tattvas, burning the bonds); 18 saṅkṣiptadīkṣā (abbreviated initiation); 19 sadyaḥsamutkrānti (initiation bringing immediate departure from the body); 20 tulādīkṣā (initiation by the balance); 21 parokṣadīkṣā (initiation of the absent and the dead); 22 liṅgoddhāra (removal of a prior sectarian mark); 23 abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher or adept); 24 antyeṣṭi (final rites); 25 śrāddha (rites for the dead); 26 sthaṇḍilapūjā (daily worship on a ritual ground; the remaining life of the initiate); 27 liṅgārcā (worship of the liṅga); 28 parva-pavitraka etc. (occasional rites; the gathering of yoginīs; rites for the guru); 29 rahasyavidhi (the secret Kula ritual); 30 mantra (the mantras); 31 maṇḍala; 32 mudrā; 33 ekīkāra (unification of the paths); 34 svarūpapraveśa (entry into one's own nature); 35 śāstrasammelana (the harmony of the scriptures); 36 āyātikrama (the descent of the scripture through the lineage); 37 upādeyabhāva (why this scripture is to be accepted; the author's account of himself)

summary: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's 'wish-gem of truth', the founding text of Navya-Nyāya, in four books (khaṇḍa) on perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony. summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); the seventh of the ten short treatises (daśa-prakaraṇa); it a thirteen-verse discrimination of realities: independent and dependent; Śrī as eternally free; souls graded in liberation and in bondage; eternal and non-eternal insentient things; and the relation of a thing to its properties (no difference for lasting properties; difference-and-identity for temporary ones). title: Tattvopaplavasiṃha
summary: Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa's 'Lion that upsets all principles', the only surviving work of the Lokāyata current. It examines in turn the definitions of the means of knowledge given by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists and Sāṃkhyas and argues that none can be established; the Bṛhaspati sūtra's list of four elements was stated only 'to reflect' (pratibimbana) what the world accepts, and even those 'do not stand when examined'. Worldly practice goes on unexamined; in it the fool and the wise are alike.

title: Tirukkuṟaḷ

It names no sectarian deity; its ethics of non-killing, abstention from meat, truthfulness, love, gratitude and renunciation are claimed by Śaivas, Jains, Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists, and as non-sectarian ('the common scripture').

title: Triṃśikā (Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā)
alt_titles: Weishi sanshi lun song 唯識三十論頌 (T1586, Xuanzang)

structure.description: 30 verses: 1–16 the threefold transformation of consciousness (store, mind, object-apprehension, with the mental factors); 17–19 cognition-only and the cause of rebirth; 20–25 the three natures and three naturelessnesses; 26–30 the path to the transformation of the basis

summary: Vasubandhu's compact statement of the whole Yogācāra system: all talk of self and dharmas refers to the transformation of consciousness in three forms, so everything is cognition-only; the three natures and naturelessnesses; and the path on which, when cognition no longer apprehends an object, the yogin abides in cognition-only and attains the supramundane, non-apprehending wisdom and the transformation of the basis.

title: Tripura Rahasya (Jñāna-khaṇḍa)

attribution.tradition: narrated by Haritāyana, conveying Dattātreya's teaching to Paraśurāma
attribution.scholarly: a late (c. 13th–17th c.) Śrīvidyā-milieu text; date uncertain

structure.description: Māhātmya and Jñāna khaṇḍas survive (a Caryā khaṇḍa is said to be lost); the Jñāna-khaṇḍa has c. 22 chapters (low confidence)

notes: Its non-dualism of self-aware consciousness is closer to Śākta/Pratyabhijñā thought than to Śaṅkara's; placed under Advaita by the registry and by modern Advaita use (e.g. Ramaṇa's circle).
summary: A Śākta-Advaita teaching in verse in which Dattātreya instructs Paraśurāma, narrated by Haritāyana; through stories such as that of Hemacūḍa taught by his wife Hemalekhā it teaches that the self is consciousness that knows itself (with the power of self-awareness, vimarśa), that the world is its reflection like an image in a mirror, and that realization is stable abidance beyond the alternation of samādhi and activity.

notes: Owned by U04; U23 adds Śrīvidyā key teachings. Text checked in sources_raw (vedaH/misc/upaniShat/shAktA; eBhāratī bhāvanopaniṣat).

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Thirty-eight verses on the three natures: what appears is the dependent, how it appears is the imagined, and the constant absence of that appearance-as-duality is the perfected; the three are both distinct and not distinct; the magical elephant illustrates them; understanding, abandonment and attainment occur simultaneously, leading to the realization of the dharmadhātu and the three bodies.

title: Treasury of Valid Reasoning (tshad ma rigs pa'i gter)
summary: Sakya Paṇḍita's verse treatise and autocommentary on epistemology restoring Dharmakīrti's intent: only particulars are real; universals, relations and 'real' generalities posited by the earlier Tibetan (Sangphu) logicians are conceptual constructions; perception is non-conceptual; the treatise organises Buddhist logic in eleven topics.

title: Tshad ma yid kyi mun sel
summary: Chapa Chökyi Senge's summary of epistemology, from which (by tradition) the Collected Topics method and the Sangphu school's acceptance of real universals derive.

title: Tsigdön Dzöd (tshig don rin po che'i mdzod, the Treasury of Words and Meanings)

title: Tsik Sum Ne Dek (tshig gsum gnad brdeg, Hitting the Vital Point in Three Words)
summary: Garab Dorje's last testament, given to Mañjuśrīmitra as the master dissolved into light: introduce directly to one's own nature; decide on one thing; gain confidence in liberation.
notes: Part of the 'last testaments' ('das rjes) collected in the Vima Nyingthig (from memory).

title: Tukārām Gāthā
summary: The collected abhaṅgas of Tukārām (about 4,500 in the standard editions): confession and struggle, the name 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari', Viṭṭhala standing on the brick, scathing attacks on hypocrisy and caste pride, the saints' company, and songs of fulfilment. The third of the Vārkarīs' three foundational books, sung daily in bhajan and kīrtan.

attribution.tradition: Tukārām's; his notebooks, thrown into the Indrāyaṇī at Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ's order, rose dry after thirteen days; Santājī Jagnāḍe and others wrote them down.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted core; the corpus was fixed in manuscripts of disciples and printed in 1873 (Bombay government-sponsored edition); some interpolations.

They teach devotion to Śiva as the liṅga, the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), the triad of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama, work as worship (kāyaka) and giving (dāsōha), and criticize caste, pollution rules, temple and Vedic ritualism and outward show in favour of lived experience (anubhava).

summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika in ten books. It announces the explanation of dharma — that from which prosperity and the highest good result — and grounds the Veda's authority; lists the nine substances, the qualities and the five motions and defines substance, quality and motion; treats being, universals and particulars, the elements, time, space, the self (with its marks and plurality) and the atomic mind; atoms and perception; motions caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); yoga and liberation; ethics of giving, food and ritual observances; inherence; absence; perception, inference and memory; and the seers' knowledge.

title: Vāk Sūkta (Devī Sūkta, Ṛgveda 10.125)
summary: Speech (Vāc) proclaims herself: she moves with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and All-gods and bears Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Agni and the Aśvins; she is the queen, the gatherer of treasures, first of those worthy of worship, placed by the gods in many places; through her one eats, sees, breathes and hears, and those who do not know her dwell beside her; whom she loves she makes formidable, a brahman, a seer, a sage; she bends Rudra's bow; she gives birth to the father on the world's head; her womb is in the waters; she blows forth like the wind, beyond heaven and earth.

title: Vākyapadīya
summary: Bhartṛhari's treatise on 'sentence and word' in three books. Book 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa) teaches that Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world, that all cognition is word-permeated, the sphoṭa–dhvani distinction, the three levels of speech and grammar as a path to liberation; book 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa) argues that the sentence is the indivisible unit of meaning, grasped as pratibhā; book 3 (Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka) analyses universals, substance, relation, quality, direction, means, action, time, person, number, gender and compounds in fourteen sections (samuddeśa).

attribution.tradition: Bhartṛhari (often identified in the tradition with the poet of the Śatakatraya)
attribution.scholarly: Bhartṛhari the grammarian; his identity with the poet of the Śatakas is doubted

title: Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra associated with the Ṛgveda. summary: An eight-limbed yoga for the twice-born framed by Vedic orthodoxy: yamas and niyamas, a few postures, the channels and kuṇḍalinī, breath-control, a withdrawal (pratyāhāra) that moves the breath through the eighteen vital points (marma), concentration on the elements, meditation and samādhi. title: Vijñānabhairava
summary: A dialogue in which the Goddess (Bhairavī) asks Bhairava about his true nature; he rejects every form 'with parts' (the ninefold, the mass of sounds, the three-headed, nāda-bindu...) as a device for the confused (vv. 7-13), describes the supreme state as indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess (14-21), and in answer to her request for means (22-23) teaches 112 contemplations (dhāraṇā) of the 'waveless state' (24-138; counted at 139). It then redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (144-153), teaches the natural 'haṃsa' repetition of the breath (154-156), enjoins secrecy (157-160), and closes with the Goddess embracing Śiva, having grasped 'the essence of the Rudrayāmala' (161-163).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to Bhairavī; claims to be the essence of the Rudrayāmala and of the Trika (vv. 1, 161-162).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous. The claimed Rudrayāmala origin cannot be verified: the early Rudrayāmala is lost, and the extant Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra) is a different and later text. Cited by Kṣemarāja, who began a commentary on it.
