CORRECTION to editions: the skeleton gave every text the same generator default, 'Adyar Library Upaniṣad series (Schrader … 1912; … with Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's commentary)'. Schrader's 1912 volume is a critical edition of twenty Saṃnyāsa texts with his own ṭippaṇī, not Brahmayogin's commentary. Brahmayogin's commentary on the Saṃnyāsa group appeared separately in 1929 (ed. T. R. Chintamani Dikshit; Muktabodha M00334 metadata; archive.org). The Adyar volume is therefore replaced with the one volume that holds this text (Sannyāsa). The years 1920, 1921, 1923 and 1925, and the editor A. Mahadeva Sastri, are confirmed on the web. The text is also among Schrader's twenty (per the archive.org full text), so his edition is kept as a separate entry. The Olivelle dating is confirmed at group level (Wikipedia, Sannyasa Upanishads). Seven older texts reach their final form between the last centuries BCE and c. 300 CE. The Āśrama is 3rd c. CE, the Nāradaparivrājaka and Śāṭyāyanīya c. 12th c., and about ten others 14th-15th c. correction_log.reason: Located in the local 120-Upaniṣad e-text (heading at line 25384 (collection no. 101)). Its place in the Muktikā canon is confirmed from the Muktikā in the same e-text: no. 97 in 1.30-39, listed under the Śukla Yajurveda in the prose Veda lists, with that Veda's peace-chant. Group 'Sannyāsa' matches the local group list. CORRECTION to editions: the skeleton gave every text the same generator default, 'Adyar Library Upaniṣad series (Schrader … 1912; … with Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's commentary)'. Schrader's 1912 volume is a critical edition of twenty Saṃnyāsa texts with his own ṭippaṇī, not Brahmayogin's commentary. Brahmayogin's commentary on the Saṃnyāsa group appeared separately in 1929 (ed. T. R. Chintamani Dikshit; Muktabodha M00334 metadata; archive.org). The Adyar volume is therefore replaced with the one volume that holds this text (Sannyāsa). The years 1920, 1921, 1923 and 1925, and the editor A. Mahadeva Sastri, are confirmed on the web. The text is also among Schrader's twenty (per the archive.org full text), so his edition is kept as a separate entry. The Olivelle dating is confirmed at group level (Wikipedia, Sannyasa Upanishads). Seven older texts reach their final form between the last centuries BCE and c. 300 CE. The Āśrama is 3rd c. CE, the Nāradaparivrājaka and Śāṭyāyanīya c. 12th c., and about ten others 14th-15th c. The tradition account (śruti, authorless) is left as it is.

summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana. It defines yoga as the stilling of the activities of the mind (1.2); teaches practice and dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and Oṃ, the obstacles and their remedies, the samāpattis and the kinds of samādhi (pāda 1); kriyā-yoga, the five afflictions, karma, the seer and the seen, and the first five of the eight limbs (pāda 2); concentration, meditation, samādhi, saṃyama, the transformations of mind and the powers with their warnings (pāda 3); and the sources of powers, karma and latent tendencies, the reality of objects, the non-self-luminosity of mind, the cloud of dharma and kaivalya (pāda 4).

title: Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

attribution.tradition: composed by Vālmīki, author of the Rāmāyaṇa, and told to Bharadvāja: the dialogue in which Vasiṣṭha teaches Rāma, with Viśvāmitra present, at Daśaratha's court
attribution.scholarly: the vulgate is a Vedāntic revision of the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya (src:moksopaya), an anonymous 10th-c. philosophical poem; its non-dualism is close to but not identical with Śaṅkara's Advaita and shares vocabulary with Kashmiri Śaiva and Buddhist idealist thought

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki; the teaching given by Vasiṣṭha to the young Rāma in the Tretā age

scholarly.text: the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. CE (Slaje, c. 950); the Vedānta-oriented Yoga Vāsiṣṭha vulgate is a later revision (c. 11th-14th c.); older proposals ranged from the 6th to the 13th c.

structure.description: 6 prakaraṇas: Vairāgya (dispassion, 33 sargas), Mumukṣu-vyavahāra (conduct of the seeker, 20), Utpatti (origination, 122), Sthiti (persistence, 62), Upaśama (quiescence, 93), Nirvāṇa (liberation, pūrvārdha 128 + uttarārdha 216). The text names itself Mokṣopāya and claims 32,000 verses (2.17.6); the printed vulgate has roughly 27,000-29,000

summary: Vasiṣṭha teaches the despondent young Rāma that the world is a projection of mind within the one consciousness (cit), arising like a dream; that human effort (pauruṣa) guided by scripture and the good overrides fate, which is only past effort; that liberation comes by inquiry (vicāra) with the four gatekeepers (peace, inquiry, contentment, holy company), by the weakening of latent tendencies (vāsanā) and the stilling of mind and breath, through seven stages of knowledge to liberation while living. The teaching is carried by dozens of stories (Līlā, Karkaṭī, Lavaṇa, Śukra, Dāśūra, Prahlāda, Bali, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Vītahavya, Bhuśuṇḍa, Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja, the stone and others).

title: Yoga Yājñavalkya

attribution.tradition: Yājñavalkya teaches yoga to Gārgī
attribution.scholarly: anonymous orthodox text dependent on the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā, c. 13th–14th c.

tradition.text: the Upaniṣadic sage Yājñavalkya

structure.description: 12 chapters (adhyāya), c. 500 verses

summary: An eight-limbed yoga for Vedic householders and renouncers taught by Yājñavalkya to Gārgī: ten yamas and ten niyamas, postures, the channels and the ten breaths, purification of the channels, breath-control with Vedic mantra, a fivefold withdrawal including the movement of breath through the eighteen vital points, the five element concentrations, meditation and samādhi. title: Yogabīja

attribution.tradition: a dialogue of Īśvara (Śiva) and Devī, ascribed to Gorakṣa
attribution.scholarly: anonymous, Nāth milieu, c. 14th c.

tradition.text: Śiva's teaching to the Goddess

structure.description: c. 190 verses (recensions vary)

summary: Argues that knowledge alone does not liberate: the body must be 'ripened' (pakva) in the fire of yoga, for an unripe body is subject to karma and rebirth. It teaches the great yoga (mahāyoga) that unites mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja, and gives what is probably the earliest statement that 'ha' is the sun and 'ṭha' the moon, their union being haṭha.

title: Yogabindu
summary: Haribhadra's Sanskrit treatise (c. 527 verses) on the qualification for yoga (the last turning, caramāvarta; the one who will not again bind the maximum karma, apunarbandhaka), the preliminaries (pūrvasevā), five kinds of religious performance (poison, venom, non-performance, its cause, nectar) and five yogas: adhyātma, bhāvanā, dhyāna, samatā and vṛttisaṃkṣaya.

attribution.scholarly: a compilation of several layers by the early Yogācāra community, the Śrāvakabhūmi among the oldest

tradition.text: revealed to Asaṅga by Maitreya

structure.description: Basic section of seventeen stages (bhūmi): 1 the five sense-consciousnesses, 2 mind, 3 with initial and sustained thought, 4 without initial but with sustained thought, 5 without either, 6 concentrated, 7 unconcentrated, 8 with mind, 9 without mind, 10 made of hearing, 11 made of reflection, 12 made of cultivation, 13 śrāvakas, 14 pratyekabuddhas, 15 bodhisattvas, 16 with remainder, 17 without remainder; followed by four compendia (Viniścaya-, Vastu-, Paryāya-, Vivaraṇa-saṃgrahaṇī)

summary: The encyclopaedic foundation of Yogācāra: an analysis of consciousness, the grounds of meditation and the paths of the three vehicles, in which the store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) is first argued for (in the Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī) and the bodhisattva's training, discipline and grounds are laid out.

title: Yogadīpikā (Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya)

structure.description: 10 paṭalas

summary: A manual in ten paṭalas by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya on yoga as the Dvaita tradition understands it: yoga is the supreme worship of Hari with devotion through prescribed action; one remembers Hari as the real agent within one's limbs; it describes the training of a devotee, study and reflection on Madhva's works, initiation by the ācārya, worship with mantra and nyāsa, contemplation of oneself as the reflection (pratibimba) of Nārāyaṇa in the heart, a graded list of disciplines crowned by hearing, reflection, meditation, samādhi and bhakti, and the presence of Hari in both the worshipper and the image.
notes: Author named in the opening and closing colophons of the raw_etexts copy; verse references checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya

tradition.text: Śvetāmbara tradition dates Haribhadra's death to 529 CE

structure.description: 228 verses

summary: Haribhadra's 228-verse treatise on yoga: three yogas (by desire, by scripture, by capacity), the eight views (dṛṣṭi) — mitrā, tārā, balā, dīprā, sthirā, kāntā, prabhā, parā — each correlated with one of Patañjali's eight limbs, the removal of a fault and the rise of a quality; the unity of the goal under many names; four kinds of yogins.

attribution.tradition: Colophon: by Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, paramahaṃsa pupil of Govindānanda; each pāda is called part of the 'sāṅkhyapravacana' and of the Yogamaṇiprabhā.

scholarly.text: late 16th – 17th c. CE (inferred from his teacher Govindānanda)

summary: A vṛtti that follows the bhāṣya (bhāṣyānugā). On 1.1 it explains 'anuśāsana': although the śāstra was made by Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, considering it extensive, begins a śāstra that follows it.

title: Yogamārtaṇḍa
summary: A haṭha text ascribed to Gorakṣa, closely related to the Gorakṣaśataka/Vivekamārtaṇḍa family of texts.
notes: Relation to src:vivekamartanda (U28) to be established; possibly an alternate title of a member of the same family. Low confidence.

title: Yōgāṅga Trividhi
summary: A short poem in tripadi metre ascribed to Akka Mahādēvi on yoga and the path to the liṅga.

title: Yogarahasya (of Nāthamuni)
summary: Nāthamuni's lost treatise on (aṣṭāṅga) yoga, which the hagiographies say he taught to Kurukai Kāvalappaṉ; the original is lost. A text published in the 20th century under this title is claimed in T. Krishnamacharya's lineage as a recovery; that claim belongs to lin:krishnamacharya and is not accepted here as the original.

tradition.text: Nāthamuni, traditionally 9th–10th c. (hagiographies give an extremely long life)

title: Yogaratnākara
summary: An anonymous late compendium of diagnosis and formulations (including mercurial ones).

title: Yogaratnamālā
summary: Kāṇha's (Kṛṣṇācārya's) 'Jewel Garland of Yoga', the classic Indian commentary on the Hevajra Tantra.

editions.name: Derge Tengyur, Tōh 1183 (confirmed in the local Derge catalogue)

notes: Sanskrit edited by Snellgrove with the Hevajra (1959); not local.

title: Yogasāraprābhṛta
summary: Amitagati's Sanskrit treatise in nine chapters on the realities and on yoga as the path, closely following Kundakunda.

title: Yogasāra (Yogīndu)
summary: Yogīndu's c. 108 Apabhraṃśa dohās on yoga as knowing one's own self to be the supreme self: 'who the supreme self is, that am I'.
notes: Title present in the local catalogue (catalog:JainDB:योगसार--योगींदुदेव); catalogue confirms extant digitized text, not author or date.

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's digest of the doctrine of the Yoga Sūtras as he expounds it in the Yogavārttika.
notes: Structure and contents not recalled in detail (gap).

title: Yogaśāstra (Hemacandra)

structure.description: 12 prakāśas, c. 1,000 verses, with the author's own commentary

summary: Hemacandra's treatise in twelve chapters (prakāśa) written for king Kumārapāla: yoga as the three jewels; the conduct and vows of the householder; conquest of the passions and senses, the twelve reflections, equanimity and the four friendly contemplations; postures; breath, the winds and signs of death (with the warning that breath-control does not serve liberation); the four objects of meditation (piṇḍastha, padastha, rūpastha, rūpātīta) with the five concentrations; virtuous and pure meditation; and a closing chapter on his own experience of the no-mind state.

title: Yogaśāstra-svopajñavṛtti
summary: Hemacandra's own long commentary on the Yogaśāstra, with illustrative stories and verses quoted from earlier works.

title: Yogaśataka (Haribhadra)
summary: Haribhadra's Prakrit hundred verses on yoga: yoga in the ultimate sense (niścaya) is the union of the three jewels in the soul, in the conventional sense (vyavahāra) their causes such as serving the teacher; the practitioner's qualification and the teacher's adapting of instruction to the student.

title: Yogasiddhāntacandrikā
summary: Nārāyaṇatīrtha's extensive vṛtti. Its opening verses give the transmission (Pitāmaha taught yoga; Śeṣa in the sūtras; Vyāsa in the bhāṣya; Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu clarified the bhāṣya) and argue that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted pradhāna's independence, not yoga as meditative cultivation; the introduction treats deep contemplation (nididhyāsana) as samādhi, 'also called rājayoga', and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Maheśvara teaches Brahmā in six chapters: knowledge and yoga together; ripe and unripe bodies; mind bound to prāṇa; the four yogas as one great yoga; two kinds of siddhi; the body as Śiva's temple; nāda and the levels of speech; devotion to the guru; channels; the suṣumnā as supreme tīrtha; the ten signs.

title: Yogasudhākara
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras ('the speech of the lord of serpents') by Sadāśiva Brahmendra, composed, as its closing verses say, by the grace of the teacher and offered at the teacher's feet.

title: Pātañjalayogasūtravṛtti (Yaśovijaya)
summary: Yaśovijaya's commentary on selected sūtras of Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra, accepting much of Patañjali's method while correcting points of doctrine (the self, Īśvara, liberation) from the Jain many-sided view.

title: Yogasūtradīpikā (Pradīpikā) of Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: A commentary 'for the easy understanding of the slow-witted' by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, who says it condenses the meaning examined in the bhāṣya and 'by my teacher himself in the Vārttika' (Vijñānabhikṣu).

title: Yogasūtravṛtti of Nāgeśa (Nāgojī) Bhaṭṭa
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras by the grammarian Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa. On 1.1 it says the śāstra expounds in detail the yoga taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and others; on 1.2 it glosses citta as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and nirodha as a special, supersensible effort that dissolves the activities.
notes: Nāgeśa is reported to have written a longer and a shorter vṛtti (Bṛhatī, Laghvī) — which one the local raw_etexts file contains is not verified.

title: The Yogāvacara's Manual
alt_titles: The Yogāvachara's Manual of Indian Mysticism as Practised by Buddhists

attribution.tradition: a yogāvacara's handbook of the old kammaṭṭhāna
attribution.scholarly: a manuscript from 18th-c. Sri Lanka connected with the Siamese ordination lineage; edited by T. W. Rhys Davids (PTS 1896), translated by F. L. Woodward as Manual of a Mystic (PTS 1916)

summary: A Sinhala-Pali manuscript manual of the old (borān) meditation: preliminary rites, the five kinds of rapture, the tranquillities and other qualities to be induced in order at points of the body, and the path attainments.
notes: Content summarized from memory at a general level only (low confidence on details).

title: Yogavallī
summary: A modern Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Sūtras. Its introduction surveys the darśanas, gives the count of 195 sūtras (51, 55, 55, 34), notes that some manuscripts mark the end of the work after pāda 3, cites the verse from Bhoja's vṛtti on Patañjali's three kinds of purification, and compares the Vivaraṇa, Tattvavaiśāradī and Yogavārttika on particular sūtras.
notes: Only the Samādhipāda is in the local raw_etexts file; author and date not identified (gap).

title: Yogavārttika

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive sub-commentary on the bhāṣya. It calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda spoken by Vedavyāsa' and holds Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas to be contained in it like rivers in the ocean (intro.); cites the Yoga-Yājñavalkya for Hiraṇyagarbha as first teacher (1.1); argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi against a single-reflection view (1.7); gives its own account of the four samprajñāta samādhis (1.17); and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (1.51).

editions.name: ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta), with the bhāṣya; e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Yogaviṃśikā
summary: Haribhadra's twenty Prakrit verses (the 17th of his Viṃśativiṃśikā): all religious activity that joins one to liberation is yoga; its five kinds — posture (sthāna), sound (ūrṇa), meaning (artha), support (ālambana), the supportless (anālambana) — each in four grades (desire, practice, steadiness, perfection). Commented by Yaśovijaya.

title: Yogaviṣaya
summary: A short tract of thirty-three verses attributed to Mīnanātha (Matsyendra): the qualified disciple, the six centres from ādhāra to ājñā, the three channels, the three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, the names of kuṇḍalinī, the nectar raining from the brahma-place, inner worship with the flower of the mind, and the haṃsa repeated 21,600 times as 'so 'ham'.

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)

notes: Colophon in the e-text reads 'matsyendranāthaviracitaṃ ...'; the text calls its author Mīnanātha, son of Umā and Śaṅkara (v. 7). Date uncertain.

title: Yogayātrā
summary: Varāhamihira's work on the timing, omens and rites of a king's military expedition, opening with a teaching that fate (karma of another birth) and human effort together bring success, and that neither favourable planets nor rites alone suffice.
notes: Local e-texts: GRETIL and Pingree's edition.

title: Yoginī Tantra
summary: A tantra of Kāmarūpa in two parts on the Goddess Kāmākhyā and the sacred geography of Kāmarūpa, the worship of Kālī and Kaula rites, with legendary material on the region.

editions.name: Muktabodha Digital Library e-text M00064

notes: Division into two parts from memory; content not checked in detail.

title: Yoginīhṛdaya
summary: The esoteric 'heart' of the Vāmakeśvara teaching in three 'codes' (saṅketa): the code of the cakra (the Śrīcakra as the emanation of the supreme Śakti and the universe of principles), the code of the mantra (six levels of the mantra's meaning), and the code of worship (three kinds of worship, inner and outer rites). Knowledge of these codes is said to make one liberated while living.

title: Verses in Praise of Amitābha Buddha
summary: Tanluan's hymn of homage in seven-character verses, each followed by 'may I with all beings be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss': Amitābha's attainment ten kalpas ago, his twelve names of light, the land and its assembly, and homage to Nāgārjuna; the model of Shinran's Jōdo wasan.

title: Kathang Zangling Ma (bka' thang zangs gling ma, the Copper Island biography)
summary: The earliest full treasure biography of Padmasambhava, revealed by Nyangral Nyima Özer: his lotus birth in Oḍḍiyāna, training, arrival in Tibet, the building of Samye, the taming of spirits, his teachings to the king and disciples and his departure to the land of the rākṣasas.

title: Song in Praise of Zazen (Zazen wasan)
summary: Hakuin's vernacular hymn: all beings are originally buddhas, like water and ice; not knowing it is near they seek it far away; the Mahāyāna zazen is beyond praise; this very place is the Lotus Land, this very body the Buddha.

title: Points to Watch in Zazen (Zazen yōjinki)
summary: Keizan's practical instructions on zazen: posture, eyes, diet, clothing; ordinarily rest the mind in the left palm — if the mind sinks, place it at the hairline or between the eyebrows, if it scatters, at the tip of the nose or below the navel; warns against visionary and other deviant states.

title: Zazengi (Principles of Zazen, Shōbōgenzō)
summary: Short instructions: a quiet place, thick mat, full or half lotus, cosmic mudrā, upright posture, breathing through the nose, thinking of not-thinking; 'zazen is not learning meditation (shūzen); it is the Dharma gate of ease and joy'.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Zazenshin (Lancet of Seated Meditation)
summary: Comments on Yaoshan's 'thinking of not-thinking… non-thinking' and on Nanyue polishing a tile; praises Hongzhi's Zuochan zhen and offers Dōgen's own version.
notes: Not held locally; paraphrases from memory, no original quoted.

title: Zen Phrase Anthology (Zenrin kushū)
summary: Anthology of Chinese phrases used as capping phrases (jakugo) in Rinzai kōan training; the 1688 edition expands Tōyō Eichō's earlier Kuzōshi.

title: Zerbu Dunpa (gzer bu bdun pa, the Seven Nails)
